Harsh Joshi
I like building products and meeting new people. I’ve worked in hospital plant rooms, on software for small businesses and on GPU clouds. At RawThoughts I test ideas in software and write down what holds up. Snoop around for the products, research and stories, and reach out if something catches your eye.

works.title: When intelligence gets cheap
works.description: Research into production, scarcity, distribution and the models we use when cognitive work becomes cheaper.

body:
Raised in Lucknow, with roots in Almora.
I studied Electronics and Communication Engineering at Dehradun Institute of Technology, under Uttarakhand Technical University, from 2012 to 2016. I also studied remote sensing and satellite navigation through IIRS. My formal training began in electronics, but my reading never stayed there. Questions about time led into philosophy and texts such as the Katha Upanishad. Building circuits and reading a dialogue between Nachiketa and Yama were different ways of spending an afternoon, yet both could leave me wondering whether I had understood the question at all.
I have bought more books than I can read, played piano, made art, trained for MMA tournaments and hiked through much of India, spending time in monasteries along the way. You could call it an extensive period of regression testing on a personal front. Work has been just as exploratory. The people I could learn from often mattered as much as the job. In an early team, I could be cleaning the office floor, testing a PCB, designing an algorithm, writing firmware, talking to a vendor or helping someone else find their way into the problem. That breadth was an education in how much surrounds the apparently technical task.
Building with other people
My first research grew from an undergraduate thesis, Project Netra, with NEFORD and ICAR-CSSRI's Regional Research Station in Lucknow. We were investigating inexpensive image analysis and embedded measurement for reclaiming sodic soil. It put the question of what a measurement means beside the people who needed to use it. During those college years I was a Google Student Ambassador and received NRDC Young Innovator and Intel Innovator recognition. The research also took me into guest lectures at IISR, IWMI in Laos, IIRS Dehradun, Pantnagar University and Allahabad University: another way of finding out whether I could make the work intelligible to somebody else.
Smart Joules grew from idea stage to Series A. I joined as its founding engineer in November 2016 and progressed to Product Development Lead, working across DeJoule, JouleLabs and JouleMind through March 2020. I also represented the work outside the plant: on the panel at NREDCAP’s Powering Andhra Pradesh summit and at Shell’s Make the Future in Singapore.
Field work in hospital plant rooms changed what I expected from engineering. The operator needed a usable control, not our internal picture of the network. At the same time, building the team meant explaining the purpose of the work and making room for people to contribute. I founded and ran JouleLabs around that connection: students and mentors working on real problems, with support that continued beyond handing over a brief.
At Zenoti, customer evidence pushed me in another direction. Support, onboarding and taxation for small businesses needed a simpler experience inside a much broader suite. I narrowed the roadmap and helped ship the redesign. Understanding more of the system let us ask less of the customer. It also changed my sense of ambition: removing the right complexity can be harder, and more useful, than adding another feature.
Finding a way to build
While I was discovering myself, I was also putting bread on the table: building ventures as an adviser and consultant, building two startups from zero as a founder, and working as a product manager in a startup that had already scaled. AI ran through all of it. I was lucky in the people I got to learn from, including people who had spent longer in the industry than I had been alive.
My work with Sachait Technologies Pvt. Ltd. grew from helping friends into cofounder responsibility for product and engineering. Emergency response made the gap between detecting an event and helping a person impossible to overlook: false alarms, human review and the next responder all belonged to the product. That work continued as YOJN Care. In October 2022, I co-founded DAO Studio with Shashwat Pandey. Amul and Lijjat Papad inspired its original ambition: help people create decentralised autonomous organisations. Exploring how AI could support that ambition led into making intelligence easier to use. I led its product, technology and company work through September 2024, and built YojnAI as an individual contributor. Composing model and tool work, inspecting the path and learning from feedback brought earlier product questions into a new technical setting.
In September 2024 I built a reflection agent for code and for structured OpenAPI and gRPC specifications with Specmatic. Later work brought me into engineering leadership at Accacia and GPU-cloud product work at AION. The settings changed what I needed to understand: an agreement between services, the meaning inside a building-material document, the cost of finishing a GPU workload. I kept product responsibility close to hands-on engineering. Organising a team did not remove my desire to understand the mechanism; it made explaining its consequences to other people more important.
My interests widened with those changes. Compute became a question about useful capacity and the economic arrangements around it. I also found myself building explanations alongside products. A writer arriving at a technical subject needs more than a title; an engineer making a product decision needs more than a summary. Finding the connection between the predicament, the mechanism and the argument became another part of the work.
A practice beyond the job
Teaching has stayed with me. I volunteer with and help lead UPAI, the Uttar Pradesh AI community. Lucknow AI Labs, or LAI, is its founding Lucknow chapter. A student's question or a collaborator's objection can reveal something I had stopped noticing. I am interested in education that gives curiosity a rigorous path, including the patience and support to follow it after the first explanation stops being enough.
Shared research asks something beyond explaining an answer. People need a question they can actually work on together, with room for different contributions and a way to examine what those contributions changed. My own curiosity has moved through geometry, time, learning and the organisation of intelligence. Across those forms, I keep asking what causes what, how I could tell, and what that understanding lets me change. Keeping an ambition alive while becoming less attached to its first explanation has been an important part of that movement.
Personal life changes the work as well. A venture that occupies every hour cannot be judged only by the elegance of its product. Relationships, family and the possibility of continuing matter. I have become more interested in what can endure, and in what remains useful when an experiment ends, without pretending that every detour was part of a plan.
Today I bring that practice to consulting at RawThoughts. Alongside it, I am building Pale so people and agents can continue work across their applications, and Gazette so connected writing, research and documentation can become publications people can explore. Agents decide far more often than people, so by the time one writes, what it read has usually changed; I am building Weave and Scope so the people and agents who share a piece of work can still act on a current picture of it. Causality takes the inquiry into adaptive models and architectures: how small reasoning units might learn to organise, and how a system can change its description of a problem. Post-AGI Economics follows what cheaper machine agency changes in production and ordinary life. The environment I want to work in is part of the construction, not simply a set of tools around it.
Art, music and cultural reading are not decorations added after the serious work. An image can make a relation visible; a sequence can change what it means; a tradition can resist the interpretation I arrived with. My graphic novel Sleepwalker gives those encounters a world to develop in. Working through different forms lets another kind of question appear. There are questions for which a working system is the right response, and others that need a proof, a conversation or an image. I would rather find the right form than make every curiosity serve a professional label.
My résumé is available on request. If you’d like to talk about the work, write to me. For a longer conversation in another form, I have spoken on The Naked Product and Strategy of Finance.

node.title: From a model answer to a useful product
node.description: Product judgment connects model behaviour to a user's task, the surrounding operation and a way to recover.

body:
From a model answer to a useful product
My earlier encounters with AI came through image processing and embedded systems. The model did its part inside an arrangement of sensors, software and people. It didn't usually offer to explain the arrangement back to me.
A language model does. Ask it a question and the component suddenly sounds like the person who understands the whole operation. It can interpret a request, explain a bill and recommend a next step. That is an extraordinary entrance to a product. But what happens when we follow the recommendation past the answer? The bill has to be the right one. The proposed correction has to reach a process that can make it. Somebody still has to live with the result.
The customer didn't arrive for our demonstration
In a demonstration, we can provide the right information, ask an intelligible question and stop at the impressive answer. A customer arrives with a situation. They may have the wrong record, misunderstand the procedure or ask for something the business cannot do. They may be returning after a failed attempt, or need somebody else's approval before acting. Their starting point is part of the product problem.
Consider a hypothetical small business trying to understand an unexpected charge. A model can explain a bill, but I would first want to decide what kind of help the product is offering. Is it an explanation, a prepared dispute or a change to the account? These are different promises. The prepared dispute might be a useful first product: identify the bill, show the disputed amount and its basis, let the customer correct the draft, then put it into an existing resolution process.
That choice changes what we build and measure. A fluent explanation of the wrong bill cannot pass merely because it reads well. A correct draft that never reaches anyone able to resolve it has also left the customer with unfinished work. Before expanding the conversation to every question about the account, I would want the narrow operation to have a recognisable end: the customer can inspect the proposed dispute and knows what happened after submitting it.
What becomes possible when the entrance changes?
The new capability can change the process around it. A business that previously required customers to know its internal categories might let them begin with an outcome. A worker might examine a larger range of alternatives because preparing each one costs less. This changes how people ask for help, what work is economical to offer and where human attention is needed, rather than merely making the old screen faster.
The move from broadcast to on-demand gives a useful comparison. Distribution technology changed what people could consume and how creators could reach them. A conversational system could likewise change the entrance to a service: the person states an outcome instead of first learning the provider's categories. The product opportunity includes that new relationship. But possibility is not adoption. A useful behaviour has to meet an actual need, and the organisation needs a way to sustain it. A feature that customers try once because it is surprising is different from work they return to because it helps.
A smaller product around a larger capability
At Zenoti, customer evidence led me towards a simpler experience for a small-business segment within a much larger suite. Understanding what the customer needed mattered more than displaying everything the product could do. AI introduces different mechanisms, but a similar product decision: a model may make many responses possible while the valuable operation remains narrow. The user might need to settle one charge, not converse about the whole account. Three consequential choices can be more useful than a seemingly unlimited assistant that cannot complete any of them.
Support, onboarding, data migration and handoffs are part of that operation. They determine whether the person can begin, whether the context is coherent and whether an exception has somewhere to go. A conversational front desk still needs those connections behind it; fluent conversation does not remove the work of completing a request.
Which part needs to get better?
A poor result can come from several places: the model misunderstands, retrieval selects the wrong source, a tool returns stale information or the business process is undefined. Treating every failure as a model problem lets us spend more on the component while leaving the cause untouched. Better training can address a recurring capability gap; a clearer source can address a retrieval problem; an explicit rule can resolve a decision the business has already settled. A narrower task or a person's judgment may be the right intervention for an exception. Technical fluency helps product work choose among these mechanisms instead of translating every objection into a demand for a more intelligent model.
Research, adaptation and operation have different work to do. Research may explore whether a capability is possible. Adaptation makes a chosen capability fit a task and its examples. Operation has to keep the resulting application usable as sources, users and dependencies change. A roadmap connects these activities through the outcome it seeks, while giving each an appropriate way to learn. Treating them as one uninterrupted process of “the AI getting better” makes both costs and responsibilities harder to see.
The economic comparison also has to follow the completed work. A cheaper call can create more retries and support, while a more expensive model can be worthwhile if it reliably removes a costly part of the process. Neither conclusion follows from the price per token alone. Specialised capability, different models within one application and deterministic software each have a place where they improve the work. The model does not need to become everything for the product to become useful.
What am I confirming when I press the button?
When an application suggests a correction to the hypothetical bill, the person needs to know what is being changed and why. A confirmation button without that context only makes the ambiguity clickable. Improving the system presents a related problem: a rating can report dissatisfaction without locating its cause, and a trace can record steps without explaining which statement is justified. In both cases, the interface needs to make the consequential parts available to judgment. That may call for a comparison, an editable draft, a source reference or a handoff, rather than another conversational turn. Reducing effort helps when it leaves the person better able to complete the task; concealing a consequential mistake takes something else away.
Beyond the impressive answer
An AI product brings a capability into an outcome someone wants, at a cost the operation can carry, with a way to recognise and repair the failures that matter. Agents and conversation contribute through the useful work they make possible. Product work, architecture and engineering meet in making that promise specific enough for somebody to try and the result specific enough to learn from. What interests me is the work that becomes possible, the people it helps and the arrangement around the model that makes it real.
The broader argument about how this changes product management follows the research, the new user behaviours and the organisation needed to build for them.

The user might need to settle one charge, not converse about the whole account. Three consequential choices can be more useful than a seemingly unlimited assistant that cannot complete any of them.
Support, onboarding, data migration and handoffs are part of that operation. They determine whether the person can begin, whether the context is coherent and whether an exception has somewhere to go. A conversational front desk still needs those connections behind it; fluent conversation does not remove the work of completing a request.
Which part needs to get better?
A poor result can come from several places: the model misunderstands, retrieval selects the wrong source, a tool returns stale information or the business process is undefined. Treating every failure as a model problem lets us spend more on the component while leaving the cause untouched. Better training can address a recurring capability gap; a clearer source can address a retrieval problem; an explicit rule can resolve a decision the business has already settled. A narrower task or a person's judgment may be the right intervention for an exception. Technical fluency helps product work choose among these mechanisms instead of translating every objection into a demand for a more intelligent model.
Research, adaptation and operation have different work to do. Research may explore whether a capability is possible. Adaptation makes a chosen capability fit a task and its examples. Operation has to keep the resulting application usable as sources, users and dependencies change. A roadmap connects these activities through the outcome it seeks, while giving each an appropriate way to learn. Treating them as one uninterrupted process of “the AI getting better” makes both costs and responsibilities harder to see.
The economic comparison also has to follow the completed work. A cheaper call can create more retries and support, while a more expensive model can be worthwhile if it reliably removes a costly part of the process. Neither conclusion follows from the price per token alone. Specialised capability, different models within one application and deterministic software each have a place where they improve the work. The model does not need to become everything for the product to become useful.
What am I confirming when I press the button?
When an application suggests a correction to the hypothetical bill, the person needs to know what is being changed and why. A confirmation button without that context only makes the ambiguity clickable. Improving the system presents a related problem: a rating can report dissatisfaction without locating its cause, and a trace can record steps without explaining which statement is justified. In both cases, the interface needs to make the consequential parts available to judgment. That may call for a comparison, an editable draft, a source reference or a handoff, rather than another conversational turn. Reducing effort helps when it leaves the person better able to complete the task; concealing a consequential mistake takes something else away.
Beyond the impressive answer
An AI product brings a capability into an outcome someone wants, at a cost the operation can carry, with a way to recognise and repair the failures that matter. Agents and conversation contribute through the useful work they make possible. Product work, architecture and engineering meet in making that promise specific enough for somebody to try and the result specific enough to learn from. What interests me is the work that becomes possible, the people it helps and the arrangement around the model that makes it real.
The broader argument about how this changes product management follows the research, the new user behaviours and the organisation needed to build for them.

notes.body_html:
What a different picture lets us ask

Imagine sending two requests before either reply arrives. The clock records when each request and reply occurred, but neither reply names the request it answers. Putting the four events in order still leaves two possible exchanges. A diagram could show which reply belongs to which request, provided we have a source for that connection. The worked example on Causality shows why more precise timestamps cannot supply the missing relation.

Now imagine claiming that the alternative picture predicts a different interval between request and reply. That claim asks more of the picture. It needs a definition of the predicted quantity and an observation that could distinguish it from the ordinary account. A representation that reveals dependence is useful for that purpose; its usefulness does not automatically become evidence for the new prediction.

Experience raises a third question. Waiting for an important reply can feel longer than doing absorbing work during an equal measured interval. The clock gives us a common comparison; the description of waiting gives us something about the person's situation. Neither is improved by pretending to replace the other. The interesting work is to understand what kind of difference the person is describing.

The dependency picture, a predicted interval and the experience of waiting consequently ask different things of the same exchange. The first needs the missing relation, the second needs a physical model and observations, and the third needs the person's situation. They can meet in one event while requiring different ways of making it intelligible.

node.title: The vocabulary of an unfamiliar world
node.description: A triangle, a clock and an operating-system image open questions that change as I follow them. What must a new vocabulary let us see?

body:
The vocabulary of an unfamiliar world
Okay, imagine joining a conversation where nobody shares your vocabulary. You can point, draw and demonstrate, but even those gestures need some agreement. A circle might mean a place, a person, a boundary or a journey. Where do you begin? Before arguing about the answer, you have to discover what the other person thinks the question is.
I keep running into a version of that predicament when I think about time. We have clocks, equations and a perfectly serviceable language for getting to a meeting. Then somebody asks what time is, and the meeting suddenly seems easier. What have those words and symbols allowed us to describe? What did we leave outside them?
A triangle with three right angles
Draw a triangle on a flat sheet. Its angles add to 180 degrees. Now start at the North Pole, follow a meridian to the equator, travel a quarter of the way around the equator and return along another meridian. The three angles of this spherical triangle are all right angles. The result is 270 degrees. Did the triangle break mathematics?
An equilateral triangle on a flat plane, with all three angles marked.
On the plane: 60° + 60° + 60° = 180°.
Great-circle arcs join the North Pole to two equator points ninety degrees apart; each surface angle is marked as a right angle.
On the sphere: 90° + 90° + 90° = 270°.
The right angles are measured on the spherical surface. Its projection onto this page changes how those angles look.
Of course not. We changed the setting and kept speaking as though we hadn't. The familiar statement came with a surface, a meaning of a straight path and a set of assumptions. On the sphere, the sides follow great-circle arcs. The surprise is useful because it makes the setting visible again. What looked like a fact about every possible triangle was a fact about a particular geometry.
That does something to my intuition about time. Perhaps a familiar picture has become so comfortable that I no longer notice what it assumes. A line orders events. A clock compares intervals. A dependency diagram shows which event relied on which other event. Waiting for a reply gives me yet another encounter with duration. These are useful descriptions, but they do not all make the same thing visible.
It is tempting to jump from the spherical triangle to a different geometry for time. I have felt that temptation. But the triangle has not told us what such a geometry would be, much less what it would predict. It has given us a better question: am I dissatisfied with the physical account, the picture I use to understand it, or the way it meets experience? Those lead to rather different work.
My early essay More than a line pushed the image into a deliberately strange thought experiment: suppose time had a fractional dimension and could be described in a non-Euclidean geometry. What would a line through that space look like? I imagined it bending, looping, disappearing and returning before it began. The image led me towards retrocausality, the possibility of an effect preceding its cause, and towards a hunch that time, chaos, entropy and consciousness belonged in a connected inquiry.
I had not constructed that geometry. Curvature, fractional dimension and causal ordering name different properties; choosing either of the first two does not establish the third. That is where the mathematical work has to begin: define the space, the dimension being used, the relation between events and what “before” means within the construction. A second, a minute and an hour give me units for comparing duration. They do not, by themselves, settle which of those questions I meant by “what does time look like?” I still want to follow the hunch far enough that its assumptions can meet a real test.
When the picture becomes the explanation
Mathematics gives us an extraordinary vocabulary. A derivative makes a rate of change something we can work with; a coordinate system lets us describe a position; a transformation lets us ask what survives a change of description. Learning the notation is not quite the same as learning to see through it. A beautifully written equation can remain as opaque as that conversation in an unfamiliar language.
I am interested in the point where a representation becomes something we can think with. Could a better description of dependence make an otherwise confusing process intelligible? Could it expose that two accounts agree only because we have forgotten how their variables were measured? Those are questions about the work a representation does, before any grand claim about discovering a new law.
My questions have become more particular as I have followed them. The early image asked whether a different vocabulary could make a difficult world intelligible. The research question now asks what a description lets me distinguish, what a change of setting does to those distinctions and how I can recognise that its language has become too small. Changing the description itself is a larger ambition than improving an estimate within it. A perfectly accurate answer can still concern the wrong-sized question.
Take two exchanges that overlap in time. A timestamp tells me when each request and reply occurred. It may leave out which reply answered which request, whether the answer resolved the question, and which later decision relied on it. A different picture can restore those relations without changing the physical intervals. If I then ask what would remain valid after a reply were corrected, the picture has another job: it has to preserve the dependencies through which the correction matters. The useful vocabulary changes as the work demands more of it.
That is the progression I want to keep following. An image suggests a question; a construction makes one part of it precise; a counterexample shows where the construction stops helping. I do not want to turn an awkward question into a polite instruction to stay within familiar categories, or ask the first metaphor to defend every explanation I attach to it. A different formalism would need to let us do something we could not do as well before. The reach of the image can survive the work of finding out what that something is.
A lifetime in a breath
Now change the observer. Imagine a lifetime passing in a breath on another scale. From inside that life, there were years of waiting, work, love and loss. From outside, barely a moment. The image unsettles me because nothing about the smaller world feels small to the person living there.
That is part of what draws me towards Markandeya recognising his own place within an impossible frame. A story can let the reader inhabit the shift. An equation would need to define its quantities and their relationship; the scene can stay with what the change of scale does to a person's sense of a life. It has a different kind of precision: which detail remains recognisable when the world around it becomes impossible?
I want both forms available. Sometimes the next step is to calculate. Sometimes it is to sit with an image until I understand why it will not leave me alone.
An operating system for intelligence?
The same habit follows me into product work. What if intelligence could be composed the way we compose software? The operating-system image opens a whole vocabulary: capabilities, interfaces, memory, applications. Suddenly there are places to ask where a useful piece belongs and how something else could use it.
Some of that has an ordinary software answer. Retain the result of a step, expose an interface and resume when the missing information arrives. That was part of the work of composing agents and playbooks at DAO Studio. Another part of the ambition reaches inside a learned model: can we find a capacity, separate it and use it elsewhere? A callback does not answer that question. We would have to understand what the capacity depends on and what changes when we move it.
Still, I would rather follow the discomfort than discard the image. Perhaps the useful abstraction is an application interface. Perhaps the capacity we hoped to compose depends on an exchange the interface never described. The comparison has helped me find both questions, provided I let the unfamiliar work change the familiar name's meaning.
That is what interests me about vocabulary. It can give a thought somewhere to begin, and then quietly become the wall it cannot get past. The answer is not always another word. Sometimes we need a different picture, an experiment or a story. Sometimes we need to return to the conversation and admit that we have been answering different questions all along.

node.title: Sneak peek into infinity: the breath of cosmos and its duration
node.description: A breath opens a thought experiment in control systems, cosmic time and unbounded ratios, leading to the possibility of collective consciousness.

body:
Sneak peek into infinity: the breath of cosmos and its duration
In the quiet moments of deep breathing, have you ever felt a subtle shift in your perception of time and reality? This experience is where I want to begin an inquiry into consciousness, reaching beyond the scale of an individual life.
It begins with a breath.
In our daily lives, breathing is an automatic function, a simple necessity of life. But when we attend to it, especially through practices such as pranayama, something ordinarily unnoticed becomes available to us. We can change the rhythm and notice how the encounter changes. It is not only meditative mumbo-jumbo: breathing practices are also used to help bring about a relaxation response. What interests me here is the connection between a physical process, our state of mind and the way time is experienced.
Give the breath an input
An engineer reaches for a model. Perhaps the duration and quality of a breath can be treated as a control signal, with a transfer function representing the process through which breathing influences consciousness. Something like

Y(t)=T\cdot X(t),

where X(t) represents the breathing pattern, Y(t) the consciousness level we would like to describe, and T the relation between them. The simplest version makes T=k, a positive constant: change the input and the output changes proportionally.
Someone with a neuroscience background could model the mechanics better than I can. I clearly do not have that background. The mind is non-linear and considerably more complicated than this constant gain; even the quantities would need research before we could measure the relationship. For now, the sketch gives me a way to ask how a physical breathing pattern might influence consciousness.
If you are particularly curious about the time variable, much like I am, the question soon becomes larger than this little equation. How do we describe all the different ways an interval can be encountered? What might a vocabulary for that question let us see? That curiosity also runs through my questions about geometry and description.
But you get the general idea of what I am trying to communicate here, right? I digress. Coming back: a change in breathing is an ordinary physical act through which we can examine a change in experience. I want to follow that connection into a much less ordinary scale.
It expands to cosmic scales
Begin with the human scale: each breath, each moment. Seconds become minutes, hours become days, and years open into yugas, mahayugas, manvantaras and kalpas. These names belong to a larger account of recurrence, eventually taking us to the life of Brahmā and the world associated with it.
Now meet the image of Mahā-Vishnu's breath. In the Brahma-saṁhitā, the lives of the Brahmās presiding over universes fall within one exhalation. A universe's entire history becomes part of another rhythm. Its creation and dissolution fit within a breath; another breath opens the possibility again.
Tale, wisdom, fiction, interpretation: whatever your angle, the image asks something rather startling of our attention. One breath contains a lifetime of worlds.
Where, in this grand scale of breath, are you? Let us choose seven seconds for a human breath. It is an arbitrary interval for the thought experiment. How many such intervals belong within the cosmic breath? What fraction of the larger duration does your breath occupy?
For any specified finite duration, we can divide by seven seconds and obtain a finite count. That is one calculation. The thought I want to follow goes further: take the cosmic scale as unbounded. There is no largest duration in the comparison I am making. The names can be variables for you; the question is the relation between an interval we can hold and a scale without a final bound.
How many zeroes are contained in an infinity?
How many twos are there in ten? Five. How many ones? Ten.

\frac{10}{2}=5,\qquad \frac{10}{1}=10.

Now ask the deliberately awkward question: how many zeroes are there in an infinity?
Your intuition probably says infinitely many. Trust your intuition, then look at what we have actually put into the fraction. The human breath was never zero. We chose seven seconds. It only began to look like zero when placed beside an ever-larger duration. And infinity is not a very large real number waiting to be divided; it names the absence of a bound.
Write B for the duration being compared, measured in seconds. The number of seven-second intervals is B/7. As the duration grows without bound,

\lim_{B\to\infty}\frac{B}{7}=\infty.

Look in the other direction and the fraction represented by one human breath tends to zero:

\lim_{B\to\infty}\frac{7}{B}=0.

It is no longer an indeterminate form. The denominator is finite and nonzero; the duration in the numerator grows without bound. The answer in this construction is infinity.
What would that mean?
With breath and time as proxies for consciousness in this thought experiment, I picture consciousness expanding towards infinity as the imagined breath extends towards the cosmic scale. Looking back towards the human scale, our individual awareness becomes a near-zero part of that expanse. The ratio gives me the scale; what follows is the possibility I see in it.
Within that picture, cosmic consciousness can be a superset of individual experiences: all forms of life, all the different encounters through which existence becomes known. Our awareness is a drop in that ocean, but a drop belongs to the ocean. Being small in the comparison has not placed it outside the whole.
You know the monkey typing on a keyboard for long enough to produce Hamlet? That is the image I reach for: an immense space of possibilities in which something as particular as a play can occur. A cosmic or collective consciousness could contain the individual forms through which we encounter it. The superset, or universal set, if you will.
But calculating the ratio and experiencing that connection are different things. Knowing, understanding and realising can take us through the same words and leave us somewhere quite different.
My early generative-art explorations for Sleepwalker gave this question another form. An image of Markandeya could hold the encounter with another scale while I worked through the calculation separately. It helps me separate the myth from the maths. The creative inquiry that grows from the breath has room for a witness, a world and the bewilderment that a ratio cannot draw for us.
The universe in our breath
The attraction of this idea is not only the size of the number. It is the possibility of meeting something immense through an act so ordinary that I usually do not notice it. The traditions of breath and meditation invite that encounter from experience; the mathematical construction gives one relation within it a form we can examine.
I see in it a connection between individual awareness and an unbounded possibility of consciousness. A small experience can remain intimate while belonging to something beyond the frame in which I first understood it. The cosmic scale does not make the breath disappear. It changes what I can imagine the breath participating in.
So, take a deep breath and remember: it begins with a breath.
The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health describes breathing exercises among relaxation techniques. That evidence concerns particular bodily and psychological effects; it does not supply a scale of consciousness for this thought experiment.
Brahma-saṁhitā 5.48, in the Bhaktivedanta edition. This is the textual image behind the comparison. Treating the cosmic duration as unbounded is the thought experiment's additional premise, not a value measured from the verse.

indexed.title: Sneak peek into infinity: the breath of cosmos and its duration
indexed.description: A breath opens a thought experiment in control systems, cosmic time and unbounded ratios, leading to the possibility of collective consciousness.
indexed.body:
Sneak peek into infinity: the breath of cosmos and its duration
In the quiet moments of deep breathing, have you ever felt a subtle shift in your perception of time and reality? This experience is where I want to begin an inquiry into consciousness, reaching beyond the scale of an individual life.
It begins with a breath.
In our daily lives, breathing is an automatic function, a simple necessity of life. But when we attend to it, especially through practices such as pranayama, something ordinarily unnoticed becomes available to us. We can change the rhythm and notice how the encounter changes. It is not only meditative mumbo-jumbo: breathing practices are also used to help bring about a relaxation response. What interests me here is the connection between a physical process, our state of mind and the way time is experienced.
Give the breath an input
An engineer reaches for a model. Perhaps the duration and quality of a breath can be treated as a control signal, with a transfer function representing the process through which breathing influences consciousness. Something like

Y(t)=T\cdot X(t),

where X(t) represents the breathing pattern, Y(t) the consciousness level we would like to describe, and T the relation between them. The simplest version makes T=k, a positive constant: change the input and the output changes proportionally.
Someone with a neuroscience background could model the mechanics better than I can. I clearly do not have that background. The mind is non-linear and considerably more complicated than this constant gain; even the quantities would need research before we could measure the relationship. For now, the sketch gives me a way to ask how a physical breathing pattern might influence consciousness.
If you are particularly curious about the time variable, much like I am, the question soon becomes larger than this little equation. How do we describe all the different ways an interval can be encountered? What might a vocabulary for that question let us see? That curiosity also runs through my questions about geometry and description.
But you get the general idea of what I am trying to communicate here, right? I digress. Coming back: a change in breathing is an ordinary physical act through which we can examine a change in experience. I want to follow that connection into a much less ordinary scale.
It expands to cosmic scales
Begin with the human scale: each breath, each moment. Seconds become minutes, hours become days, and years open into yugas, mahayugas, manvantaras and kalpas. These names belong to a larger account of recurrence, eventually taking us to the life of Brahmā and the world associated with it.
Now meet the image of Mahā-Vishnu's breath. In the Brahma-saṁhitā, the lives of the Brahmās presiding over universes fall within one exhalation. A universe's entire history becomes part of another rhythm. Its creation and dissolution fit within a breath; another breath opens the possibility again.
Tale, wisdom, fiction, interpretation: whatever your angle, the image asks something rather startling of our attention. One breath contains a lifetime of worlds.
Where, in this grand scale of breath, are you? Let us choose seven seconds for a human breath. It is an arbitrary interval for the thought experiment. How many such intervals belong within the cosmic breath? What fraction of the larger duration does your breath occupy?
For any specified finite duration, we can divide by seven seconds and obtain a finite count. That is one calculation. The thought I want to follow goes further: take the cosmic scale as unbounded. There is no largest duration in the comparison I am making. The names can be variables for you; the question is the relation between an interval we can hold and a scale without a final bound.
How many zeroes are contained in an infinity?
How many twos are there in ten? Five. How many ones? Ten.

\frac{10}{2}=5,\qquad \frac{10}{1}=10.

Now ask the deliberately awkward question: how many zeroes are there in an infinity?
Your intuition probably says infinitely many. Trust your intuition, then look at what we have actually put into the fraction. The human breath was never zero. We chose seven seconds. It only began to look like zero when placed beside an ever-larger duration. And infinity is not a very large real number waiting to be divided; it names the absence of a bound.
Write B for the duration being compared, measured in seconds. The number of seven-second intervals is B/7. As the duration grows without bound,

\lim_{B\to\infty}\frac{B}{7}=\infty.

Look in the other direction and the fraction represented by one human breath tends to zero:

\lim_{B\to\infty}\frac{7}{B}=0.

It is no longer an indeterminate form. The denominator is finite and nonzero; the duration in the numerator grows without bound. The answer in this construction is infinity.
What would that mean?
With breath and time as proxies for consciousness in this thought experiment, I picture consciousness expanding towards infinity as the imagined breath extends towards the cosmic scale. Looking back towards the human scale, our individual awareness becomes a near-zero part of that expanse. The ratio gives me the scale; what follows is the possibility I see in it.
Within that picture, cosmic consciousness can be a superset of individual experiences: all forms of life, all the different encounters through which existence becomes known. Our awareness is a drop in that ocean, but a drop belongs to the ocean. Being small in the comparison has not placed it outside the whole.
You know the monkey typing on a keyboard for long enough to produce Hamlet? That is the image I reach for: an immense space of possibilities in which something as particular as a play can occur. A cosmic or collective consciousness could contain the individual forms through which we encounter it. The superset, or universal set, if you will.
But calculating the ratio and experiencing that connection are different things. Knowing, understanding and realising can take us through the same words and leave us somewhere quite different.
My early generative-art explorations for Sleepwalker gave this question another form. An image of Markandeya could hold the encounter with another scale while I worked through the calculation separately. It helps me separate the myth from the maths. The creative inquiry that grows from the breath has room for a witness, a world and the bewilderment that a ratio cannot draw for us.
The universe in our breath
The attraction of this idea is not only the size of the number. It is the possibility of meeting something immense through an act so ordinary that I usually do not notice it. The traditions of breath and meditation invite that encounter from experience; the mathematical construction gives one relation within it a form we can examine.
I see in it a connection between individual awareness and an unbounded possibility of consciousness. A small experience can remain intimate while belonging to something beyond the frame in which I first understood it. The cosmic scale does not make the breath disappear. It changes what I can imagine the breath participating in.
So, take a deep breath and remember: it begins with a breath.

node.title: Debauchery, in the name of existence!
node.description: A year-end provocation about solving problems, transferring their consequences and making room for compassion and unfamiliar ways of knowing.

body:
Debauchery, in the name of existence!
A provocation from the end of 2019.
History. Sound. Ideas. What do they have in common? I kept seeing cycles: peace and violence, crests and troughs, a return that our confident accounts of progress had not prepared us to recognise. Periodicity seemed almost a property of existence itself. Life was a montage of the ripples that existence left behind, and we were rarely still enough to notice what repeated.
It remained important to strive for peace. Oblivious to the ripples, the cycle continued.
Are we solving the problem?
We take pride in calling ourselves problem solvers, innovators and explorers. But if a wave washes the sand from beneath my feet while I watch the sunset, does witnessing the spectacle make me an explorer?
Why ask such an absurd question? Meh. No reason. Except that I wanted to challenge the flattering premise beneath those names.
What if much of what we called solving a problem was a transformation of its presentation? We took an unpleasant present and moved it into a less familiar, more enticing future. The future inherited the consequences, while the present celebrated the ingenuity of the translation.
That was not necessarily easy work. It could require extraordinary engineering, organisation and imagination. The objection was that being difficult did not settle whether it had solved the problem. A civilisation could become very accomplished at changing the form in which its difficulties arrived.
Businesspeople, engineers, doctors, lawyers, teachers, scientists and statespeople all participated. We divided the planet with fences, colours, weapons and beliefs, then kept fighting the wars of people no longer alive. Generations of martyrs raised further generations. When trust became scarce, cooperation looked increasingly like another game. Somehow, like cockroaches, we survived.
The uncomfortable possibility of being wrong
I thought of Phoebe challenging Ross in Friends: could he leave even a little room for the possibility that he was wrong? The appeal was in the challenge to his certainty. A sitcom exchange is a poor history of science, but it can be an excellent mirror for intellectual vanity.
Artists seemed more willing than many of us to admit that they did not know what the hell they were doing. An artist could stay inside a question without first dressing it as a result. I found that courage valuable.
Enlarge the window beyond one lifetime and our professional confidence can begin to look peculiar. We understand some intricate details and still struggle with the elementary questions. What is consciousness? Do the needs of the many outweigh those of the few? What is the nature of existence? We move between quantities, convictions and competing ways of giving the question meaning.
I was frustrated by how quickly that difficulty could become a reason to stop listening. Citations could be treated as a substitute for understanding the claim they supported. A reference to a Vedic practice could be dismissed before anyone had asked what kind of account it offered.
Which vocabulary gets to enter the conversation?
Consider the five koshas, or sheaths, described in Vedantic accounts of a person. Or the yogic vocabulary of ida, pingala and sushumna. These names do not become anatomical structures simply because someone draws a parallel with nerves or glands. Yet I wanted room to ask what the descriptions were doing before deciding that their failure to fit an anatomical vocabulary made them worthless.
My provocation was that science, too, was another belief system, albeit one in which consistency and elegance were paramount. I wanted to challenge the confidence with which we could dismiss an unfamiliar account while treating our own frame as the only one worth inhabiting. The comparison did not establish that every inherited claim was true. If we could be sceptical of an unfamiliar claim, surely we could also examine the certainty with which we had decided what was worth hearing.
The question of vocabulary irritated me: how could this conversation recognise its own assumptions if its words already settled what could count as an answer?
The thing we let loose
We create technologies and ideologies, then release them into a world whose responses we cannot fully anticipate. Greed can outrun compassion. Confidence in the evidence we possess can outrun our understanding of what will happen once other people begin using the creation.
Should we create something knowing that it could be used for great evil? The question deserves more than a template answer. A calculation can illuminate a consequence, but somebody still chooses what belongs in the calculation. A belief can sustain a commitment, but somebody still lives with what that commitment permits.
We no longer have to stone a philosopher to make a difficult question unwelcome. There are quieter ways to keep it out of the room. Oblivious to the ripples, the cycle continues.
The silence between the vibrations
We seek symmetry in history, sound and ideas. I was interested in the stretches of silence between the vibrations: what the impression of continuity made us overlook. A coherent story could offer a sense of knowledge and control while hiding how much we had simply carried forward into another form.
That was my worry about innovation. Beyond the question of securing the next investment, what had we understood about the problem's survival? Had we changed the conditions producing it, or transferred the burden to a person or generation outside the frame?
A game organised around survival does not automatically give us exuberance. Yet we keep rolling the dice, enjoying the next little rush, while the possibility of losing remains somebody else's difficulty. Debauchery, in the name of existence.
All that anger came back to a modest wish: more compassion, and a more peaceful new year. Solving a problem ought to include the lives that continue after our account of the solution ends. I wanted us to look at those lives before celebrating how cleverly we had moved the problem.

node.title: Dumb comedy: existentialism for the twenty-first century
node.description: Why sitcoms, their awkward heroes and the small pleasure of a joke gave me a way back into larger questions at the end of 2019.

body:
Dumb comedy: existentialism for the twenty-first century
Written at the end of 2019, with a new decade approaching.
Yup. That is exactly what it sounds like. I root for Ross. I root for JD. I root for Marshall, Leonard and Phil. Different people in different sitcoms, yet there is something familiar about their predicament: the outlier, the geek, the person everybody is comfortable laughing at. The adorable ones.
Their plight makes me think about education and its place in society. Its fall feels like our biggest unpatched bug. We leave room for a character to be foolish, persistent and oddly perceptive on television. Around our water coolers and balconies, we are less patient with somebody whose question does not fit the conversation. We discuss proposals, law, ethics, experience and philosophy as though the boundaries between them were obvious. Meanwhile, the supposedly dumb ones keep trying to clear the haze for whoever comes next.
Why am I talking about this? Because it may be one of the few things on which I can agree with a lot of people. Stretch most other conversations over a decade and they start to resemble horror stories.
New year, same difficult whys
The point of “New Year, New Me,” surely, is to look at what we have created before deciding what we will create next. Get your priorities straight, as the old man would put it. Have your whys in order.
This little nugget comes from a Certified Scrum Master. If you have no idea what that means, you lucky bastard. In a nutshell: consensus is tricky. 😉
One of my largest lessons of the decade was that a teacher need not have the form I expected. There are sayings about the student becoming ready and the teacher appearing. A sitcom could supply a small version of that encounter. It could show me something I had become too serious to notice in myself.
And if you don’t believe the horror-story bit, look around at what is happening to democracies. Not just between people and governments, but between corporations and governments, and corporations and people. Don’t even get me started on the last one. I agreed with Socrates’ criticism of democracy: he had good reasons to distrust our collective judgement. That unpatched bug in education kept making the old fellow look right.
Who makes the monsters?
But there is a ray of hope too. The war on ego and ignorance is on all fronts; the hardest is often the one I have with myself. Conflict can produce art. Artists exploring this existence are leading the change, reaching millions in ways more profound than institutional policy. People are finding art in all sorts of things.
We have been so busy looking for monsters and heroes in our electronics-powered algebraic intelligence (God damn Electricity as a Service) that we forget how we create both every day. It is a privilege to remain insulated from what people do to other people and their data, then find worse monsters and better heroes in a world made from pixels. We pay for that world every month. The same day, the same time. Exercising our privilege when it matters is a choice too.
The privilege is not itself the whole moral question. What do I do with it? When does it let me avoid something I should face, and when does it give me enough room to continue?
Isn’t that what war comes down to: the ruthless calculus of survival and submission? We work to feed ourselves and our families, to have an occasional drink and a little room for pleasure. Then comes the old question: who saves the hero?
Enjoy the little things
Perhaps this is where the memes help. Zombieland gives me rule 32: “Enjoy the little things.” I keep returning to it.
Dumb comedy is not necessarily easy. Sometimes it performs the hardest job: giving a person a small reprieve without demanding that they solve existence first. A joke lets me live and fight another day for whatever the larger work was about. It need not pretend that the work has gone away.
History, I kept thinking, is written by the victors. What we do tomorrow will be part of it the day after. A little reprieve lets us return to that struggle instead of being swallowed by it. You can be a monster or a hero, both or neither. Just don’t be an asshole to the ones who choose differently, and we can sit back to watch this little documentary play out a decade from now.
Some rules are made of glass, not rubber. Be careful when you break them. A reminder to enjoy a small thing is one I would rather keep.
What would Phil Dunphy do?
For me, entertainment is supposed to entertain. Sometimes I want it to take me away from the reality I took a break from, rather than return that reality in a more elaborate costume. The heist of a heist of a heist can wait.
When I feel the familiar anxiety gathering, I take a breath and ask myself what Phil Dunphy would do. I learn from the master, then return to the what and the how.
Pro tip from the holiday version of me: leave the whys to the holidays. And remember, nothing good ever happens after 2 a.m. If you have a PhD in sitcoms, be kind and pass the references along.
I had finally got my hands on Jean Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation. I planned to go through it over the holidays, hoping to clear some of the haze. Also, what’s your take on Rick and Morty and existentialism?

The argument began in September 2024 as the second part of a reflection on building products. Its predictions describe the direction I was arguing for then; the model examples belong to that period.
A product manager who understands the customer but cannot follow what the technology makes possible is increasingly working with half the picture. The reverse is just as limiting. Knowing a model's architecture does not tell us why somebody would return to the product tomorrow.
My argument is that every digital product manager now needs to become an AI product manager. Not because every product needs a chatbot, but because AI can change the behaviour the product serves, the work behind it and the business that sustains it. Treating the subject as a feature that another team can add later leaves those choices to chance.
From flipping pages to scrolling feeds
Remember when the programme schedule told us when to watch, and television ratings helped decide which programmes could continue? Compare that with opening YouTube or Netflix and finding a selection arranged for you. The viewer's choices, the distribution system and the business's measures have all moved.
The newspaper-to-feed transition makes the change almost comically physical. We moved from turning pages to scrolling down a screen. A thumb's new habit rested on touchscreens, networks, ranking systems, recommendation research and years of adoption. It was not just a designer choosing a different direction for the same page.
Personalised feeds made relevance and engagement part of a continuing interaction. Product work had to translate frustrations with static or irrelevant content into questions that engineers and researchers could address. Which content should appear, in what order, for whom, and what would count as a better result?
The shift was visible in use. In a survey conducted in 2020 and published in January 2021, Pew Research Center found that 86% of US adults got news from digital devices at least sometimes, including 60% who did so often. Those are distinct measures, not a single interchangeable adoption percentage.
Streaming had grown too, without already becoming all television. Nielsen's August 2020 account put streaming at a quarter of television viewing in OTT-capable homes; Netflix and YouTube accounted for 34% and 20% of that streaming time. The denominator matters. The change in the product opportunity does not need an inflated account of how complete the transition was.
The research changes what can be built
My own route through AI began closer to image processing and embedded systems than to a conversational window. Looking across the field, the sequence from LeNet's digit recognition to AlexNet, BERT and large language models shows how research changes the kinds of product questions we can ask.
AlexNet's 2012 paper described a convolutional network with 60 million parameters and an efficient GPU implementation. BERT, introduced in 2018, made bidirectional language representations useful across tasks such as question answering and language inference. GPT-3 in 2020 explored a 175-billion-parameter model whose tasks could be specified through instructions and examples in text. The first LLaMA family in 2023 ranged from 7 billion to 65 billion parameters and made a different scale-and-efficiency comparison possible.
Those are changes in architecture, training, data and use, not a league table in which more parameters automatically means a better product. By September 2024, the arrival of reasoning-oriented models was pushing my expectations further. I saw an expanding space of tasks that software might handle. A result on a particular benchmark still cannot establish that a model reasons better than a human at everything, or that its result can be trusted in the workflow we are building.
The product manager needs enough understanding to ask where the advance matters. Can the user begin with an intention instead of a category? Can a worker examine alternatives that were previously too expensive to prepare? Does a smaller specialised model make a useful operation economical? A technical change becomes a product opportunity when we can connect it to somebody's work.
The iPhone was a product argument
The iPhone is useful to me as an example of empathy meeting technical construction. The 2007 introduction brought phone, media and internet functions together around a large multi-touch interface. It changed what the screen and software could ask of the user's fingers. The opportunity was larger than making a physical keyboard slightly better.
That does not require pretending Apple invented every touchscreen or that the entire ecosystem appeared on the first day. The App Store followed in 2008. Hardware, software, developer tools and distribution became parts of a larger arrangement through which other people could build.
What interests me is the work concealed by the experience. Research, interface design, patents and engineering have to meet before a complicated system can feel natural. The customer does not need a tour of each component to benefit from it. Product judgement has to understand enough of those components to make the natural experience possible.
The same thought appears in Nike's appeal to the person becoming an athlete. The material and construction matter because of the experience they enable. The product does not become meaningful merely by reciting its technical properties.
What new habits might AI make possible?
Personalisation is one direction. In its 2018 survey, Accenture reported that 91% of respondents were more likely to shop with brands that recognised them and supplied relevant recommendations. That is a reported preference in a particular survey, not a guarantee that every attempt at prediction will be welcomed.
The ambition I was describing goes beyond ordering a familiar catalogue. A service might anticipate the next useful step, prepare a relevant option or carry the context of an unfinished task across devices. Imagine beginning on a phone and continuing in a car or at home without reconstructing the intention each time. That is a product hypothesis about continuity; making it useful also requires the person to understand and control what is carried across those settings.
Another direction is less visible technology. Think of a service such as Swiggy meeting the operating system through an action or notification instead of requiring every interaction to begin with a tour of its app. AI could make more capabilities available where the need arises. The further possibility is an “intelligence store”: capabilities that other products can call and compose, rather than a separate app for every narrow interaction.
These possibilities ask product managers to guide research towards behaviour worth enabling. Seamlessness is not a substitute for that judgement. The fact that two systems can connect does not establish that a person wants them connected, or that the resulting service helps.
Think through the system, not only the feature
In an enterprise product, a model may connect processes that already have their own rules, records and users. It could help interpret a request, prepare an analysis or move information between teams. The apparent intelligence sits inside a system that still needs consistent identities, compatible versions, current data and a way to handle exceptions.
This is why I want product managers to practise systems thinking. The engineering remains engineering; a product manager does not become its substitute. But a roadmap needs to recognise dependencies instead of treating each visible feature as an independent promise.
A framework such as the V-model offers one useful habit: connect a requirement to how it will be checked, from the whole system down to the parts. For an AI-assisted operation, that means deciding what the user must be able to complete and what evidence would show that the model and surrounding software support it.
The teams also need a shared vocabulary. We already translate a business concern such as daily active users into engineering questions about traffic, capacity and latency. Model performance needs a similarly explicit relationship to product objectives. Accuracy on which cases? A response time measured from which event? An improvement for which customer task? If research, engineering and the business each mean something different by “better,” the roadmap can advance while the product stands still.
Human review must have something to review
Control belongs in the experience. A person may need to inspect a recommendation, correct an assumption, stop an action or recover from a bad result. Validation and rollback cannot remain reassuring words attached after the main flow has been designed.
Nor does a model's fluent explanation necessarily reveal how it reached the answer. Useful transparency gives the reader the evidence, assumptions and proposed consequence they can actually examine. In the bill-dispute example, a person needs to see which bill, which amount and why a correction is proposed. A generic confirmation button asks for trust without providing the basis for it.
The appropriate review depends on the decision. A suggestion and an irreversible change need different controls. Product management has to make that distinction part of the operation, working with the people responsible for its risks and recovery.
A roadmap has to outlive the demonstration
The first useful version should leave room for the system to grow. That means understanding which capabilities can be composed, which assumptions are tied to one model and what later integrations would need. The App Store analogy matters here because the larger opportunity came from an environment in which other products could operate.
It does not mean predicting every future model. A modular design gives us places to learn and replace something without pretending the surrounding workflow has no dependencies. We still need to know what a change does to the user's experience, cost and ability to recover.
Feedback supplies one route to improvement. Reinforcement learning from human feedback is one technique; collecting reactions is not itself a training process. The product has to make the feedback interpretable, decide what it should influence, and compare a proposed change before releasing it. A complaint could point to a model weakness, a wrong source, a confusing interface or a business rule the user dislikes. Training on all four as though they were the same problem would hide the work we needed to do.
This is the move towards research management that I meant. Product managers need to help researchers choose questions tied to real customer difficulties, while keeping room for work whose value is not yet a feature on next month's plan. The conversation goes both ways: research can reveal a possibility the original roadmap did not know to ask for.
The business result is part of the product
Retention, efficiency and operating cost give the technical work an economic purpose. In their 2015 account of Netflix's recommender system, Carlos Gomez-Uribe and Neil Hunt estimated that personalisation and recommendations together saved more than a billion dollars a year, through effects including reduced churn. That was their company estimate for the combined system, not the value of one algorithm or a return another business can assume.
The relationship is the useful lesson. A recommendation matters because it helps a member find something worth watching and return to the service. A developer tool matters because it helps the developer complete work. A cheaper model call is not an operating saving if it creates enough retries and support to outweigh it.
Consumer empathy and technical fluency meet at that level. One helps us understand the work somebody values. The other helps us shape a system that can deliver it. Research expands what might be possible; engineering and the business have to make the result usable and sustainable.
That is why I do not think an “AI-powered” label is an adequate ambition for a product manager. The work is to help shape new behaviour, connect the capability to a real outcome and keep the technology from becoming the customer's burden. Don't be a generic “AI-powered” product manager. ;)

node.title: Figuring things out, one book at a time
node.description: A February 2020 reflection on forgiveness, attachment, friendship and taking time to find the next part of a life.

body:
Figuring things out, one book at a time
From February 2020: a pause, a new place and a great many unread books.
In hindsight, there is no other way but to be okay. Some experiences define you; some refine you. All of them teach you something, even when you would rather have received the lesson in another form.
I kept returning to the idea of choosing love over hatred. It led me towards forgiveness, and towards a question I had not dealt with as patiently as I imagined: what about forgiving myself before trying to forgive what had wronged me?
I had only skimmed the Heart Sutra. I was reaching for a connection, not claiming to have understood the text. There was still a book to read, a life to examine and a considerable distance between recognising an appealing sentence and knowing what to do with it.
When the remedy becomes another injury
How far can I go to fix something that seems broken? Until the remedy becomes worse than the disease? Until the broken thing consumes the person trying to repair it?
Straightforward questions, slippery ground. Before deciding how far to go, I had to ask why I felt compelled to fix it. Why this attachment? Why this insistence on deciding that something was broken, and that I was the person who needed to make it whole?
The answer I could reach was a willingness to conform to what I loved: a person, a relationship, an idea or the self I wanted to maintain. Love could have many forms. It could be directed towards a partner, a teacher, parents, friends or family; it need not have a person or even a form as its object. What I called true love asked for something less possessive than making the object agree with my idea of it.
That was easy to write. Living it was another matter.
Acceptance and forgiveness
Straightforward is often mistaken for easy. The two are not reliably correlated, let alone causally joined.
I wanted to get beyond the exhausting court in my head: right and wrong, good and evil, fair and unfair. Yet I could not simply float above it. First I had to distinguish accepting what had happened from forgiving it, and both from approving it. A fact could be undeniable while my relationship to it remained unsettled.
I found attachment to identity at the centre of that difficulty. I worked hard to maintain an account of myself. Every wound then threatened more than the immediate relationship; it threatened the account. Explaining myself again could become another attempt to make the other person preserve it for me.
There was a difference between closing my heart to stop the pain and forgiving so that the pain could fade. Neither arrived because I had found a sufficiently neat paragraph about it. I was trying to understand what I could release without pretending that the experience had meant nothing.
People remember how an encounter felt as well as what was said. Another explanation is not always another kindness. That was a difficult lesson for somebody who kept reaching for words.
The choices inside the grand explanation
Why bring trouble upon ourselves when life is already complicated? Why press the self-destruct button? A television monologue can make the question funny, or at least recognisable: we keep doing the thing that hurts, then celebrate the relief when it stops.
The image I kept from The Matrix was Morpheus showing Neo a path he could not walk for him. Yes, another reference. But it got at something I needed: somebody could offer an insight, and I could still have to choose what to do with it.
Add self-obsession, a little narcissism and a healthy dose of the God complex, then look again. The grand account of existence dissolves into small choices. What do I do next? Which response do I repeat? What do I let another person be without requiring them to support my explanation of myself?
Those easily overlooked choices mattered to the pursuit of happiness more than the size of the theory I built around them.
The family I discovered
I was grateful for the friends and family who had stayed beside me. I had not thought very hard about friendship before. I assumed it was mostly a matter of choice. Looking back, it felt more like something we had discovered over time: neither person could simply appoint the other to the role and make it true.
Living away from our families, I had not noticed exactly when friends became family. I was lucky. And, as a sitcom mother would remind us, families are embarrassing. If they never embarrass you, have they really completed the qualification?
At that moment in 2020, I was taking time off to work out the next part of my journey. A new place, the same family and extraordinary friends. The books, at least, were in abundant supply.
So I decided it was time to forgive, and to keep figuring things out one book at a time. The later question of detachment would take another form. Here, it began much closer to home: what could I stop demanding from a hurt, so that the rest of life could continue?
