node.title: When the compute question became larger
node.description: Following useful AI capacity from a workload into the organisations and economic arrangements around it.

body:
When the compute question became larger
I began looking at AI infrastructure partly through the market: what was being built, where the constraints were, and what an investment in that change might really be exposed to. The question became harder to hold at that distance. To understand the market, I needed to understand the work the machines could complete. To understand that work, I had to look beyond the machines again.
An hourly GPU price is an appealing place to begin because it looks comparable. But a team does not want an inexpensive hour in isolation. It wants enough suitable capacity, at the right time, to carry a workload to a useful result. The memory, network, schedule and recovery path all become part of what it buys. The completed job is a different economic object from the advertised hour.
That was the first change in my own inquiry. I had started by looking for an investment account of the AI-infrastructure market. Following procurement forced me to change the unit I was comparing. A reservation and an elastic allocation could quote the same kind of hour while asking the buyer to carry different kinds of risk. Availability, a deadline and the ability to recover unfinished work could reverse the apparent bargain. I became more interested in understanding that reversal than in producing another list of attractive providers.
The machine sits inside a process
Consider an illustrative team preparing a model evaluation for Friday. Capacity available on Saturday is not equivalent to capacity ready on Thursday, even if it is cheaper and faster once it starts. A wait changes the sequence of experiments, the time colleagues can use the result and the work that follows. Buying compute begins to look less like buying a commodity and more like arranging a process.
Inference adds a different pressure. A person waiting for an answer cares about how the service behaves under arriving demand. The same total throughput can accompany very different waiting times. The service around generation changes which capacity is useful, how much must be held ready and which apparent optimisation simply moves the cost to someone else.
These questions made engineering and economics harder to separate. A better execution arrangement can change the cost of an experiment. A better purchasing arrangement can make an otherwise impossible experiment available. Neither tells us whether the resulting capability will be adopted, who can afford it or how an organisation will change around it.
A cheap capability can meet an expensive complement
Suppose, as a thought experiment, that producing a competent document analysis becomes almost free. Its use can still depend on access to the document, a person able to judge an exception, a customer willing to change a process and an institution that accepts the result. The scarce part may have moved rather than disappeared.
At national scale, power, cooling, connectivity, access and the ability to turn output into productive work become harder to leave outside the account. That is the tension behind my India infrastructure inquiry. An announcement can describe an input while leaving the arrangement that makes it useful unresolved. Following the arrangement led me into questions about who captures value, which dependencies endure and what an expanding capability actually changes.
This is where the subject widened into organisations and their complements. Lowering the cost of one task can change the division of work. It can also leave the existing organisation largely intact because another constraint still matters more. I became interested in telling those situations apart before declaring a new era on the strength of the component.
The infrastructure collection I was exploring did not stay one collection. Some questions became technical writing, others remained procurement and policy questions, and the larger economic ones grew into Post-AGI Economics. What had begun as a way to understand a market became a way to question the account of growth itself. I no longer wanted the engineering to be background colour for an investment thesis. I wanted to know which economic conclusion the engineering could actually support.
A transition has more than one clock
The attraction of a single measure is real. A clock would offer a way to locate ourselves inside a change that otherwise feels too large to see. One Yardstick grew around that ambition. Working through the question made the differences between frontiers more important: a model can gain a capability before a firm has access, and a firm can gain access before it can rely on the capability in a valuable workflow.
The time between those frontiers depends on what changes next. An improved model, a price change or a different institutional arrangement can alter the path itself. A clock has to account for those different transitions to make the larger change easier to examine. Which measures can do that remains part of the inquiry.
The economic consequence also depends on who owns the relevant assets and how income moves. Increased productive capacity is one part of that account; the ability to buy, access or share what it produces is another. Productivity and purchasing power meet in a real economy, but they do not become the same quantity because the technology connecting them is impressive.
The inquiry has taken me further from selecting winners and closer to understanding which question a model can answer. Sometimes a changing parameter is enough. Sometimes a different constraint becomes binding. Sometimes the actors or arrangements have changed so much that the old description leaves something essential out. That movement, from the price of a machine to the adequacy of an economic account, is what keeps this work open for me.

node.title: Holding an idea without becoming it
node.description: Why detachment complements capitalism: hearing the objection, changing the plan and making room for work neither side could do alone.

body:
Holding an idea without becoming it
When I wrote about a school of unlearning, detachment from the outcome was central to the idea. I wanted to follow that thought into a less expected setting: capitalism. My argument is that detachment can make business more cooperative, because it lets us notice possibilities that a contest over our identities keeps closing.
Bring an idea into a room and watch what happens. Someone says it will never work, and suddenly you are defending much more than the proposal. There were months behind it, perhaps a career decision, perhaps the hope of finally building something of your own. They seem to have dismissed all of that in one sentence. Or did they? They may have noticed a dependency you missed. The conversation has become personal before either of you has worked out what the objection was.
That ordinary, expensive confusion is part of why detachment interests me. I want to care deeply about the work without making it responsible for proving who I am. It sounds straightforward until the idea on the table is mine.
The drive that becomes attachment
In the original 2024 essay, I called trauma the root of human motivation and creativity, and argued that it could drive extraordinary work when channelled well. That was the psychological hypothesis behind my business argument. I was trying to understand what happens when an experience shakes the beliefs a person has built their life around: a betrayal, a humiliation, a loss, or a rejection that looks trivial to everybody else.
The size of the event from outside does not tell us how deeply it reaches into that person’s beliefs. Calling someone a snowflake avoids that question. Hurt can become a reason to make something happen, to prove oneself or to build a different life. Attachment to that purpose can supply enormous persistence. It can also make an unprofitable or unsustainable path feel impossible to leave, because changing the plan now feels like surrendering the person it helped us become.
That is the tension I wanted detachment to address. The drive can remain while the plan changes. I can want to build something without asking its success to settle every earlier hurt. Otherwise a business disagreement inherits a much older argument, and the person across the table may have no idea they have joined it.
What did they actually say?
Imagine showing someone a plan for a new product. They say, “This will never work.” Perhaps they see a genuine distribution problem. Perhaps they have seen something superficially similar fail and are importing that history. Perhaps they are frustrated with the way the proposal was presented. The response can concern the idea, reveal the speaker's assumptions and comment on the person receiving it, all within the same sentence. Separating those possibilities gives the discussion an object we can examine.
There are two tempting shortcuts: dismiss the speaker because they do not understand, or treat the force of their response as evidence that the proposal is wrong. Both avoid separating the objection from the story surrounding it. Asking “What specifically would prevent it from working?” gives us something to examine. An answer about customer behaviour can be investigated; an answer about a missing capability can change the plan. Even a vague objection can reveal that the idea has not been communicated well enough. Detachment creates room for that examination without supplying its answer.
Calibrate for the error
Robotics gives me a useful comparison. The command I send and the motion an actuator produces can differ. If I insist that my command is ground truth about the machine, the machine will never work as I intend. I need to observe its response and understand the error. The point of calibration is to let the difference change what I do next.
A conversation also has a transmission, a medium and a reception. I know what I meant to say; the other person received something through particular words, timing and circumstances. Their response is evidence about that encounter. It is not a direct readout of my intention, any more than my command is a measurement of the actuator's motion. People bring histories and meanings that the machine analogy cannot contain, but the comparison gives me a useful place to start: what crossed the gap, and what did I assume had crossed it?
I cannot diagnose the person from their objection. I need enough distance to distinguish criticism of the idea, the speaker's assumptions and a comment on me. They are three different things, even when I initially hear them as one attack.
That is the calibration I want to practise. Asking which part of the proposal failed to convince someone gives the conversation something more useful than defending the whole of myself. Not everything is about me. An uncomfortable truth, and occasionally a considerable relief.
Listening without preparing the defence
There is a peculiar form of listening in which I hear only enough to construct my reply. I am present in the conversation, but most of my attention is already in the argument I intend to make. The cost is informational as well as interpersonal: the objection might contain the part that would have saved the team weeks of effort, and I am too busy defeating it to notice.
A similar investment can gather around an explanation. If a picture of time made a difficult question feel intelligible, finding a flaw in it can seem to threaten the question itself. I might protect the picture by explaining away the flaw, or dismiss the whole inquiry because its first formulation failed. Both responses give that formulation too much power. I can let the explanation change while continuing to ask what made the question worth following. The distinction gives curiosity somewhere to go after the attractive answer stops helping.
I can disagree with an objection while still letting it finish. I can revise a mechanism without surrendering the purpose. I can retain an intuition while admitting that the current explanation is inadequate. Not everything has to be a zero-sum game, or a choice between being entirely right and entirely wrong. As Obi-Wan would have it, only the Sith deal in absolutes. Humans are more than zero and one.
Two firms, one useful possibility
Detachment also changes how I think about cooperation in business. A transaction can divide something that already exists, but a collaboration can make something possible that neither side could produce alone. Suppose one small firm understands the customer's operation and another can implement a missing component. Combining those strengths could produce useful work, yet each may worry that contributing knowledge will make the other stronger at its expense.
That concern can be real: a contract, a commercial boundary or the decision not to collaborate may be necessary. There is also a different obstacle, when each firm becomes so committed to being the complete solution that neither recognises the other's contribution. They protect their standing and lose the opportunity. Distance helps me distinguish what I need from the identity I have built around how I obtain it. Owning every component, winning every argument and receiving every credit are not always the same as achieving the outcome I care about.
This is the sense in which I say detachment complements capitalism. It makes room for a non-zero-sum game: the useful work we can create together may be larger than the advantage either of us can protect alone. I do not need everyone to become a hermit for that to work. I need the question “What can we make possible?” to remain audible when “What is mine?” starts shouting over it.
Recognising that possibility does not mean trusting every promise. A collaboration can displace costs, reflect unequal bargaining power or conceal exploitation behind apparently generous cooperation. Whether it creates additional value, who receives it and what each participant knowingly accepts need examination. Those questions ask more of us than either “competition is bad” or “the market will sort it out.”
Keeping the purpose, changing the plan
Detachment is sometimes presented as withdrawal from ambition. I find that too simple. A leader who can change a plan may be more committed to the mission than one who cannot. A founder who lets a vehicle end may preserve more of the original purpose than one who keeps it going on promises it can no longer keep. The form can change while the commitment survives.
Changing direction at every objection is not openness either. An idea needs enough persistence to encounter reality; some criticism is mistaken, and some resistance reflects a worthwhile disruption. Distance should make those reasons clearer rather than make commitment impossible. I have to listen, separate the claims, return to the purpose and decide, then stand behind the decision without turning it into a permanent portrait of who I am.
The person across the table
People speak from different histories. A past failure can explain the urgency of an objection without settling whether it applies to this proposal. I can take that urgency seriously and still ask what, specifically, it reveals about the work. The person does not have to be reduced to a psychological explanation for the idea to receive a fair hearing.
Cooperation needs participants who can distinguish the shared work from a contest over themselves, as well as compatible capabilities. Making room for the other person's account, asking for the concrete concern and returning together to the purpose are everyday ways of practising that distinction. Detachment does not remove the stakes; it gives us a chance to see what they actually are.

node.description: Why possessing an explanation and making its meaning part of one's life are different encounters.

body:
Knowing, understanding and realising
Suppose, for a thought experiment, I tell you that a thousand children die every day for want of clean water. It is a terrible number, but a number you can put down and continue with your day. Now imagine those thousand bodies on the road you take home. Then hold that scene across ten years: ten times 365 times a thousand. Finally, imagine recognising somebody you love among them. The information has acquired a relation to your own life. What happened to its meaning?
Knowing, understanding, realising. We use the words almost interchangeably, yet there is a whole distance between those encounters. I can repeat an accurate explanation and remain strangely untouched by it. Another encounter can make that distance impossible to maintain. I am trying to find words for the change, not a universal staircase everyone climbs in the same order.
The useful distance of an abstraction
Knowing can be accurate, useful and uneventful. I can remember a number, repeat a definition or recognise a pattern without having a profound experience. Much ordinary work depends on precisely that ability. An engineer needs to reason about a plant without experiencing every consequence of every component all at once.
But an abstraction gives us something by leaving something else out. A map can let me find a place without giving me its life. A description of a ritual can name its sequence without telling me what participating means to someone. I can read an explanation of a passage and retain its conclusion while missing the question that made the passage important. Each representation makes a particular encounter possible. Its usefulness can also make the omitted part easy to forget.
The omitted part sometimes changes the decision. A command that looks successful on a screen matters because equipment and people depend on the physical result. A resolved ticket matters because a person was trying to finish something. Recovering that context is not sentiment added after the technical work; it can change what the technical work is for. In another setting, returning to a familiar book with an unfamiliar concern can change which passage holds my attention. The material did not need to change for my relationship to it to become different.
Understanding can become a hiding place
Understanding gives the fact a structure. Why did the temperature change? What happens if the pump is turned down? Why does a passage return to an image that seemed incidental on the first reading? How does the order of a story change what I inferred from it? An explanation lets us predict, compare and identify missing connections instead of merely repeating what we have heard. The relation gives the remembered fact somewhere to work.
Yet an elegant explanation can become a place to hide. I can explain how an organisation overwhelms its team and still reproduce the pattern. I can describe what makes a product difficult while continuing to value it mainly for its sophistication. Understanding the arrangement does not automatically settle my relationship to it: which costs I accept, which consequences I overlook, what I am willing to change.
By realising, I mean the point at which that relationship becomes harder to evade. The meaning is no longer merely an object I can describe. I am implicated in it. Emotion may accompany the change, but intensity is not what makes the interpretation true. A vivid experience can mislead as well as illuminate. The important movement is from holding a description to encountering what the description means in a life.
When the explanation comes back to me
Smart Joules and Zenoti brought technical systems and the people using them into focus for me in different ways. Components communicating mattered, but so did what an operator could understand and do with the result. A roadmap mattered, but so did the customer trying to run a business rather than navigate the product. The technical account becomes stronger when it can recognise those purposes.
Realisation need not produce an immediate visible action. A person may need time to change a habit, may lack the power to act or may discover a conflict they cannot yet resolve. An action can express an inward change without measuring all of it. Turning realising into doing would lose the very difference I am trying to name.
That distinction also makes room for patience with others. Explaining something more clearly may help them understand it without giving them my relationship to it. They have their own history, responsibilities and conditions for acting. Repetition alone cannot make those differences disappear.
Murti, darshan and the missing translation
The distinction draws me towards darshan and the experience of a murti. Translating the latter simply as “idol” can leave out the encounter I am interested in: how meeting a form might become something other than knowing its description. The person brings familiarity, practice, expectation and history; two people can stand before the same form and have different encounters. I am interested in that accumulated relationship, in how a form can hold more than the particulars a stranger sees at first glance. The visible object can remain while the encounter changes through a person's life.
I take that difference seriously without making the experience certify every explanation attached to it. Something can be transformative and still invite examination. Meaning is diminished both when we dismiss the encounter as nothing and when we demand that it prove a universal claim.
This is one reason I move between technical explanation, reflective writing and creative forms. A diagram can reveal a dependency. A scene can make its consequence present. A question can expose the assumption that held both together. In Markandeya's encounter, recognising his own hermitage within the impossible world gives its cosmic scale an intimacy that a nested diagram would omit. I can understand the containers without meeting that recognition. The scene gives me another way to approach what the description means.
Writing can make the distance between a statement and its meaning harder to overlook. It need not make every fact emotionally overwhelming. It can recover enough of the world behind an abstraction that our decisions are not made entirely inside it.

Knowing, understanding and realising
Suppose, for a thought experiment, I tell you that a thousand children die every day for want of clean water. It is a terrible number, but a number you can put down and continue with your day. Now imagine those thousand bodies on the road you take home. Then hold that scene across ten years: ten times 365 times a thousand. Finally, imagine recognising somebody you love among them. The information has acquired a relation to your own life. What happened to its meaning?
Knowing, understanding, realising. We use the words almost interchangeably, yet there is a whole distance between those encounters. I can repeat an accurate explanation and remain strangely untouched by it. Another encounter can make that distance impossible to maintain. I am trying to find words for the change, not a universal staircase everyone climbs in the same order.
The useful distance of an abstraction
Knowing can be accurate, useful and uneventful. I can remember a number, repeat a definition or recognise a pattern without having a profound experience. Much ordinary work depends on precisely that ability. An engineer needs to reason about a plant without experiencing every consequence of every component all at once.
But an abstraction gives us something by leaving something else out. A map can let me find a place without giving me its life. A description of a ritual can name its sequence without telling me what participating means to someone. I can read an explanation of a passage and retain its conclusion while missing the question that made the passage important. Each representation makes a particular encounter possible. Its usefulness can also make the omitted part easy to forget.
The omitted part sometimes changes the decision. A command that looks successful on a screen matters because equipment and people depend on the physical result. A resolved ticket matters because a person was trying to finish something. Recovering that context is not sentiment added after the technical work; it can change what the technical work is for. In another setting, returning to a familiar book with an unfamiliar concern can change which passage holds my attention. The material did not need to change for my relationship to it to become different.
Understanding can become a hiding place
Understanding gives the fact a structure. Why did the temperature change? What happens if the pump is turned down? Why does a passage return to an image that seemed incidental on the first reading? How does the order of a story change what I inferred from it? An explanation lets us predict, compare and identify missing connections instead of merely repeating what we have heard. The relation gives the remembered fact somewhere to work.
Yet an elegant explanation can become a place to hide. I can explain how an organisation overwhelms its team and still reproduce the pattern. I can describe what makes a product difficult while continuing to value it mainly for its sophistication. Understanding the arrangement does not automatically settle my relationship to it: which costs I accept, which consequences I overlook, what I am willing to change.
By realising, I mean the point at which that relationship becomes harder to evade. The meaning is no longer merely an object I can describe. I am implicated in it. Emotion may accompany the change, but intensity is not what makes the interpretation true. A vivid experience can mislead as well as illuminate. The important movement is from holding a description to encountering what the description means in a life.
When the explanation comes back to me
Smart Joules and Zenoti brought technical systems and the people using them into focus for me in different ways. Components communicating mattered, but so did what an operator could understand and do with the result. A roadmap mattered, but so did the customer trying to run a business rather than navigate the product. The technical account becomes stronger when it can recognise those purposes.
Realisation need not produce an immediate visible action. A person may need time to change a habit, may lack the power to act or may discover a conflict they cannot yet resolve. An action can express an inward change without measuring all of it. Turning realising into doing would lose the very difference I am trying to name.
That distinction also makes room for patience with others. Explaining something more clearly may help them understand it without giving them my relationship to it. They have their own history, responsibilities and conditions for acting. Repetition alone cannot make those differences disappear.
Murti, darshan and the missing translation
The distinction draws me towards darshan and the experience of a murti. Translating the latter simply as “idol” can leave out the encounter I am interested in: how meeting a form might become something other than knowing its description. The person brings familiarity, practice, expectation and history; two people can stand before the same form and have different encounters. I am interested in that accumulated relationship, in how a form can hold more than the particulars a stranger sees at first glance. The visible object can remain while the encounter changes through a person's life.
I take that difference seriously without making the experience certify every explanation attached to it. Something can be transformative and still invite examination. Meaning is diminished both when we dismiss the encounter as nothing and when we demand that it prove a universal claim.
This is one reason I move between technical explanation, reflective writing and creative forms. A diagram can reveal a dependency. A scene can make its consequence present. A question can expose the assumption that held both together. In Markandeya's encounter, recognising his own hermitage within the impossible world gives its cosmic scale an intimacy that a nested diagram would omit. I can understand the containers without meeting that recognition. The scene gives me another way to approach what the description means.
Writing can make the distance between a statement and its meaning harder to overlook. It need not make every fact emotionally overwhelming. It can recover enough of the world behind an abstraction that our decisions are not made entirely inside it.

body:
When customers need less product
Imagine buying software to make running your business easier, then discovering that your first task is to understand how the software company thinks. Its categories, configuration and navigation all make sense to somebody. Unfortunately, that somebody isn't you yet. The capability you need may be in there, surrounded by decisions you never expected to make.
Adding the missing feature gives a roadmap something obvious to say. Removing a burden asks a more awkward question: why did we make the customer carry it in the first place?
At Zenoti, I owned support, onboarding and taxation for the US and Canadian small-business market. Customer evidence led the work towards a simpler experience, rather than a better demonstration of the suite's breadth.
The work hiding in the support queue
I brought five years of support data together with product analytics, surveys and customer conversations. The breadth of the queue helped expose recurring friction; the conversations helped explain what customers were trying to accomplish when it appeared. The two forms of evidence could challenge each other. A frequently reported issue might look like a missing feature until the customer's account revealed a confusing decision or an external dependency.
“I cannot get started” brings several possible problems into the same queue. A customer may need an integration, be waiting on another provider or face incomplete imported records. They may also be able to complete the operation but struggle to find it. The diagnostic work connects the complaint to those causes: what exists, what is discoverable and which dependency prevents completion? Grouping tickets makes a recurring area visible; understanding the customer's task gives the roadmap a reason to change it.
Enough for this customer
The suite served a broader range of businesses than the SMB experience needed to expose. A capability useful elsewhere could impose configuration and navigation here without enough benefit. The segment's work gave us a way to decide which complexity was necessary, rather than treating the suite's full breadth as the natural starting point for every customer.
The evidence changed our roadmap in that direction: retain the requirements that mattered and reduce the surrounding burden. Buddy, the AI-first design system behind the revamped SMB experience, brought assistance and analytics into that narrower arrangement. The product reached customers, with self-onboarding and simpler taxation work among the changes I drove. The point of the revision was a more usable operation for this segment, rather than a smaller display of the same decisions.
Two routes to the same business operation place either the suite's categories or the customer's necessary decisions first.
This conceptual comparison keeps the necessary choices and external dependencies in both routes.
This was not a general campaign for minimalism. A business with more complex operations can genuinely need a broader arrangement, and a smaller interface can conceal a necessary dependency. The product decision is about fit: the customer should not have to absorb the whole suite merely because the company knows how to build it.
Who is doing the onboarding now?
Turning an implementation team's work into a customer checklist can relocate the burden instead of removing it. The queue disappears from one part of the organisation, but the customer still has to interpret the configuration and coordinate its dependencies, now alone. Useful self-onboarding changes the work: avoid an unnecessary decision, explain the context of a necessary one and provide a route through an exception. The customer gains a way to begin, rather than an obligation to perform the implementation team's ideal procedure.
Payment onboarding makes the distinction concrete. The software can be ready while the provider still needs to complete its part. Data migration has a different dependency: a customer's email or phone may appear in several records, so a convenient match can merge people who should remain distinct. Preserving source customer IDs helps carry identity across the import; balances and appointments then need to remain attached to the right person. The customer encounters all of this as one business operation, even though the causes and remedies sit in different places.
Learning the system just to file the tax
Country-, case- and tax-code-specific work can ask a business operator to become an interpreter of the system's internal requirements. Streamlining that work meant reducing unnecessary translation between the customer's task and the product, so they could spend less time on manual filing and compliance inside it. Removing fields helped only if the remaining experience made the important decisions intelligible. A default that changes an obligation or payment still needs to be understood; an exception still needs a navigable path. Fewer screens can follow from that understanding, but they cannot supply it.
After the ticket closes
A resolved ticket can mean that a workaround was supplied, a configuration changed or a defect repaired. To understand the customer's experience, we need to follow what happened afterwards: could they finish the operation? A falling ticket count might reflect less friction or people giving up on asking. A faster setup among those who finish might coexist with more people abandoning it. Each measure sees one part of the work.
The useful comparison follows the customer through a defined task. How many begin, where do they stop, which exceptions require help and can they complete the work they came to do? The task, customer group and period give the measures a meaning. The revised experience reached customers, but understanding its effect requires following their work through those stages rather than treating the rollout itself as the result.
Knowing enough to ask less
Choosing what the customer should not have to understand is part of product judgment. Technical fluency exposes the dependencies; customer understanding helps determine which of them belong in the experience. The two forms of work meet when a simpler path keeps consequential choices intelligible while letting the person spend their attention on the business they came to run.
That lesson has stayed relevant as models make more responses possible. A more capable component does not require a more expansive product surface: the valuable operation may remain narrow, even when the model can talk about almost anything. Sometimes the stronger roadmap is the one that understands enough to ask less of the customer.

body:
Navigating the feedback loop
An exploration of causality and awareness in AI, first published in October 2023.
I have been keeping busy following my own advice since I last published. IYKYK ;)
I've set up an experiment across publications, ventures and digital identities. Each gives me a different way to approach the same inquiry: the fundamental nature of causality, and what understanding it could make possible for artificial intelligence. A practical application, a mathematical question and a story can reveal different parts of that problem. The point of connecting them is to let what happens in one change what I ask in another.
Awareness is all you need
The practical starting point is YOJN and DAO Studio's ambition to make AI accessible, usable and available for more people to build with.
“Awareness is All You Need” is the thought I am following. Here, awareness concerns context: how a model is being used, what the task means and why particular training choices or hyperparameters have been selected. Making that setting available to the system could make its response more relevant to the work. This is a proposition about useful context, not a claim that supplying it gives a model conscious experience or settles everything an AI system needs.
The question changes what I want from an application. Producing an answer is one thing; fitting that answer into the situation that gave rise to the question is another. YojnAI gives that inquiry a practical home.
Metadata and meta-awareness
We keep hearing that data is the new oil. Perhaps the metadata is where some of the value is hiding.
Data arrives with circumstances: where it came from, what it describes and what someone intended to do with it. Those circumstances can be lost when everything becomes another training example. My interest in metadata is the possibility of carrying more of that setting into learning, so that the model has a finer account of the task rather than merely more material to process.
That is the sense in which I am exploring meta-awareness. The information about the information becomes part of the question. Whether it helps has to be shown on the task.
Intelligence that can travel
The larger ambition is to commoditise intelligence: make it as accessible and ordinary to use as electricity. Transfer learning offers a route towards that ambition, because learning need not begin from nothing for every application.
The promise is that something learned in one setting can help in another. It is not a guarantee of seamless transfer across arbitrary domains; transferred knowledge can also make the new task worse. The research on negative transfer makes that limit concrete. The interesting work is discovering what can travel and what the receiving task still needs.
The Red Pill follows the economic possibility: what changes when intelligence itself can become something people exchange? The engineering question underneath it is how that reuse could work.
Engineering the unknown
An application gives an abstract idea consequences. Something is built, someone tries to use it, and the result returns information that the original explanation did not contain. That feedback is part of the exploration, not merely the last stage after the thinking is finished.
Sleepwalker, myths and mathematics
Sleepwalker approaches causality through fiction, mythology and scientific ideas. Its protagonist's journey through feedback loops offers another way to encounter awareness: a story can let someone inhabit a question before they can express it formally.
Mathematics asks something different of the same curiosity. Natural phenomena have repeatedly prompted new mathematical descriptions. Causality is where I want to investigate the tools available for describing these relationships, their limits and the language we might still need.
The crossing between myths and mathematics matters to me. A myth can open an unfamiliar way of seeing; a mathematical account has to make its relationships precise enough to examine. Sleepwalker can explore the space between them without the story becoming proof of the scientific claim. Each form gives the inquiry something the other cannot supply on its own.
DAO Studio: the practical playground
DAO Studio is where the questions meet engineering and where an attractive account has to confront what can actually be made useful. Ideas from these different explorations can be put to work, and the next attempt can begin with something the previous one taught us. The abstract and the concrete keep meeting here.
A place to follow the crossings
getHarsh is the personal digital identity through which I catalogue and share these experiments. I think of it as decentralised in that the work has several homes: DAO Studio's practical work, Causality's research, Sleepwalker's fiction and RawThoughts' writing and discussion. Their connection is the inquiry travelling among them; each keeps its own purpose.
The loop comes back to the person asking the question. A practical difficulty can send me towards mathematics. A story can make a question vivid enough to pursue. An explanation can invite another person to notice what I missed. Publishing makes those crossings available for discussion, so that the next question need not come only from me.

node.title: How research becomes a reading path
node.description: An editorial programme connects a reader's problem to explanations, evidence and useful artifacts without turning each article into the same sales pitch.

body:
How research becomes a reading path
A person searches for a cheap GPU because that is the part of the problem they know how to name. The problem may be a delayed experiment, a growing inference bill or a model that will not fit the available hardware. A page can answer the price query accurately and still leave that person almost where they started. The more interesting editorial question is how to help them recognise what they are actually trying to decide.
At AION, I worked across GPU-cloud product questions, technical research and developer experience. I also drove a research-led content programme, connecting audience positioning, article briefs, writer coordination and technical review. The work made me think about how infrastructure becomes useful to the people building with it, and how that understanding can travel through a product or an explanation.
That made me interested in content as a programme rather than an output queue. Research has relationships inside it: a claim depends on a mechanism, a comparison depends on a common unit, and a useful recommendation depends on conditions that may not hold for this reader. Writing gives those relationships a form somebody can encounter. A programme gives them somewhere to continue when the first answer changes the question.
I find the important editorial choice comes before the writing assignment. Is this piece helping someone choose, explaining a mechanism, or giving them a method they can try? If I cannot answer that, commissioning more words only postpones the confusion. Once I can answer it, the same research may call for a short argument, a careful technical explanation or a worksheet rather than three articles competing to say everything.
The query is an entrance
Imagine planning an independent set of articles for a team trying to understand its growing AI infrastructure bill. Search results suggest a familiar inventory: hardware prices, inference optimisation, training costs and provider comparisons. The inventory is useful evidence of the language people use. It is a poor substitute for understanding their predicament. A reader comparing accelerators might need a rate card; another might need to discover that their cost is dominated by repeated preparation, idle commitment or an unsuitable workload.
An editorial choice begins to emerge once those situations are separated. One piece can make the unit of comparison intelligible. Another can follow the memory and scheduling mechanism behind a serving constraint. A worked calculation can let the reader substitute their own assumptions. A procurement question can expose a condition that a published table leaves unanswered. These are different contributions, even when they share the same search vocabulary.
The distinction changes the use of search research. It can reveal unclear terminology, recurring questions and explanations that leave a gap. It need not dictate a collection of near-identical articles built around every variation of a phrase. Google's people-first content guidance asks whether the work adds original value and helps its intended audience, rather than merely summarising existing material for search traffic. That gives the programme a useful editorial test.
Search brings a reader to a question. The writing should leave them with a better account of the question, even if that account is less convenient for the publisher's initial pitch. Otherwise the programme rewards entry while neglecting understanding.
Different readers can meet the same mechanism
A technical subject does not require a choice between an opaque engineering manual and an executive story with the mechanism removed. The same piece can begin with a consequence that matters, develop the mechanism producing it, and show what follows for a decision. The transitions need to be real. Appending a business paragraph to a technical explanation does not automatically connect them.
For example, a discussion of serving memory becomes commercially interesting when it explains how memory constrains concurrent work. A discussion of waiting becomes operationally interesting when it identifies the point at which the whole allocation is usable. A discussion of cost becomes technically useful when it states what workload and output the money buys. The reader does not have to inspect every implementation detail to understand the consequence, but the reasoning must be available to someone who does.

I would rather give a reader one satisfying explanation and a meaningful continuation than stretch every piece into an encyclopedia. The first answer should be complete enough to help on its own. The continuation is for the new question it has made visible, not for information withheld to force another click.
A brief carries the thought across people
Once other writers enter the programme, a title and a word count carry very little of the research. They identify an assignment without explaining what would make it worth reading. A writer needs to understand the reader's situation, the particular argument, the evidence available and the unresolved question. They also need room to find a better formulation than the one the initial brief supplied.
Consider a brief for an article comparing two infrastructure arrangements. “Explain why our option is cheaper” fixes the conclusion before the comparison exists. “Find which costs change when the workload is interrupted” gives the writer a real investigation. They can discover that a lower rental rate is outweighed by recovery, or that interruption is inexpensive for a restartable workload. The resulting article can teach something specific. If it contradicts the hoped-for pitch, that is editorial information the publisher needed.
Here is how I would turn that independent comparison into a brief, using invented assumptions for the example.
Part of the brief	The work it gives the contributor	
Reader	A team whose experiment can restart, but whose deadline cannot move	
Decision	Whether a lower hourly rate is worth interruptions and repeated setup	
Comparison	Cost and completion time for the same workload, including failed attempts	
Evidence needed	The interruption conditions, restart time and billing treatment, rather than a rate card alone	
Useful artifact	A two-option worksheet with visible assumptions and a deadline column	
Open question	When does the recommendation change if restart time doubles?	
The worksheet gives each contributor something concrete to improve. A specialist can challenge whether the restart assumptions fit the workload. A writer can make the decision intelligible before introducing the arithmetic. A designer can reveal which cost belongs to which attempt. If nobody can fill in the deadline column, the missing information becomes obvious before it is concealed by a persuasive conclusion.
The brief is therefore a meeting place, not a frozen script. Its purpose is to let research survive the handoff without making the contributor a transcription service. The writer's judgment and attribution remain part of the work.
Review follows the claim
The most polished paragraph can be the least trustworthy part of an article. It may contain a number borrowed from a different population, a comparison with mismatched units or an impressive example whose underlying source cannot be found. Reviewing only the bibliography misses these transformations. The question is what the source supports at the point where the article uses it.
In the hypothetical infrastructure programme, a cheaper rate does not mean a cheaper completed workload. A faster local operation does not mean a faster service. A proposed feature does not become a customer result because it has acquired a convincing narrative. An editor can make the writing more useful by making each claim smaller or more particular. The reader can then use the explanation without inheriting the publisher's wishful thinking.
Review also asks what the reader can now do. Perhaps the article gives them a question to take into a purchasing conversation, a way to interpret a measurement or an experiment they can adapt. A download or a long reading session can suggest interest, but the useful contribution is more specific than either. A programme learns when readers bring back a confusion, a counterexample or a new problem that its current explanations cannot carry.
The programme acquires a shape
There is no need for every article to repeat the whole argument. Once the pieces have distinct work, their connections become more natural. A broad economic question can lead into a calculation; a calculation can expose a technical constraint; the constraint can lead to an operational comparison. Some readers will take that path. Others will arrive at the calculation directly and leave with what they needed. The programme should accommodate both without pretending that every visitor is taking one prescribed journey.
The writing can support a commercial conversation by making it more informed. That is a different ambition from pushing every piece toward the same offer. Sometimes a reader learns that the product is suitable; sometimes they discover a limitation that should change the purchase. Trust grows in that encounter with reality, not in the absence of inconvenient information.
What I want from research-led publishing is that accumulation. An article answers a question well enough to become useful. Another gives the answer greater reach or exposes its limits. The artifacts allow the reasoning to travel beyond the original prose. Eventually the programme contains more than a record of publishing activity: it contains a way for people to think through a difficult part of their work together.

node.title: Leading beyond the title
node.description: The uncomfortable work of earning trust, making a decision and helping a team outgrow its dependence on you.

body:
Leading beyond the title
I have had amazing mentors, colleagues, friends and family, and one hell of a team. These are lessons from working with them and watching leadership emerge, including the times I got it wrong. I expect to learn better. But one thing has stayed with me: there is no nine-to-five switch for the responsibility. The people and consequences do not disappear when the meeting ends.
That is what makes leadership hard. I think of it as an art, with the balance to be found for yourself and your team. I want the work to succeed, and I want to be useful to the people doing it. Those wishes can pull in opposite directions when being useful starts to mean being needed for every decision. The harder achievement is helping the team grow beyond that dependence, then being glad that it has.
Whose ambition are we building?
A vision can be wonderfully clear inside my head and mean very little to the person I am asking to spend their life on it. What are they hoping to become? What are they giving up to be here? The company has objectives, but a team is made of people with purposes of their own. The interesting work is finding a direction they can recognise themselves in, not making my explanation so persuasive that their differences disappear.
At Smart Joules, my responsibilities grew from engineering into building and leading a product-development team. Hardware, software, research, testing, production and design could not each succeed in isolation. A technically correct component could still leave another team with an unusable system. People needed to understand the larger consequence of their decisions, not only the task assigned to them.
That kind of shared context takes time. It includes explaining why something matters, hearing where the plan does not fit and changing the division of work when the original assumptions were wrong. It cannot be replaced by a more inspiring slogan.
I think of the leader as the guardian of that vision, rather than its owner. The people doing the work give it life. Making the objectives clear is necessary management; leadership also asks whether the arrangements we built yesterday can carry today's problems, leaving the team room to build for tomorrow. If everyone is permanently fighting the present emergency, another ambitious roadmap has not given them a future.
Trust makes that possible. I have described leadership as an act of love, which may sound out of place beside a roadmap. But people are giving their time and hope to the work. A policy cannot substitute for the trust between them. Build it through honest conversations, with your guard down; if there is none, be willing to walk away. Empathy includes recognising that everyone brings experiences and boundaries of their own. It takes practice, and getting it wrong sometimes is a reason to keep learning, not to pretend the personal part can be removed.
Somebody still has to decide
There is always another projection we could prepare, another framework we could consult. Sometimes it would genuinely improve the decision. Sometimes it is how I postpone admitting that the available information will not make me certain. Waiting has consequences too. Experience can suggest a connection I cannot yet articulate, and it can make an old pattern feel applicable where it isn't. I need that intuition, but I also need to tell the team which part is a judgement and what would make us reconsider it. Otherwise my confidence becomes somebody else's unexplained risk.
Confidence that hides uncertainty borrows trust from the people who will bear the result. Endless hesitation asks those same people to carry the absence of a decision. The commitment needs to fit what the situation warrants now, with a way to learn quickly enough for the next decision to be better. Neither confidence nor hesitation removes that responsibility.
Agreement about a direction also differs from giving everyone the decision they wanted. A difficult choice can leave real disagreement. Buy-in means people understand why the choice was made, have had a chance to surface what it misses and can see how their work contributes from here. Seeking that commitment asks more of a leader than demanding consensus. It takes some distance from the plan to hear an objection without treating it as disloyalty.
When the result is embarrassing
Failures belong to the leader and success to the team: I hold that as an ethic about where to stand, rather than a literal account of who caused every event. People still have responsibilities, and causes still need examination. The leader's part is to remain present when the result exposes the direction or support they provided.
Success makes generosity easy. I can give the team credit and still enjoy how well the outcome reflects on me. Failure asks something less flattering: can somebody tell me that my direction was wrong without first taking care of my feelings? A requirement may have been unclear, the support insufficient or the promise unreasonable. If people have to protect my image before they can explain the failure, I have made the next decision harder for everyone.
Absorbing the blame helps little if everyone leaves reassured but carrying the same broken arrangement. We still need to understand what happened and who can change it. I want accepting and learning from failure to become inviting enough that people do it, including me. Run away from every failure and it begins making the next decision for you. Celebrating what we learned is part of making it possible to act again, rather than waiting until we can promise never to be wrong.
The team that no longer needs me for everything
Being needed can feel like proof that I am doing a good job. It is also an excellent way to become the bottleneck. Suppose somebody owns onboarding but has to ask me before changing a confusing step, speaking to support or investigating why customers leave. What have I actually given them? Perhaps the responsibility for reporting the problem, while keeping the useful decisions for myself. Delegation asks me to share the context and room to act, then stay available when the problem exceeds that arrangement.
Delegation becomes real when the person can carry the decision and understand where its limits are. Review can then examine the work instead of reclaiming every choice. Over time, the team should develop enough shared context and capability to do important things without the leader being the indispensable interpreter of everything. Making myself less necessary is part of building something that can continue.
There are people outside the mission, too
Leadership can involve difficult choices, personal sacrifices and work that will not fit a tidy routine. Family, support and the ability to ask for help belong in that picture; they are part of what lets someone carry the responsibility. That does not make exhaustion a measure of devotion. People have lives outside the mission, including the leader, and heroic availability can hide weak planning or inadequate capacity.
I have also worried about the difference between stopping work and recovering from it. For an entrepreneur, time away can leave the same demands running in the background. The question is whether that time actually restores the person who has to return, not merely whether the calendar calls it a break. I have no universal routine to offer; the distinction I want to keep visible is between being off the clock and being recharged.
Some commitments demand more than a comfortable routine; continuing others in the same way destroys the people making the work possible. I cannot settle that boundary for every situation. I want to know whether the sacrifice serves a purpose people understand, whether it is shared honestly and whether there is a path beyond the emergency. The leader may need support rather than another occasion to appear strong, and the people providing it bear consequences of their own.
After the title
Across employment, consulting and ventures, my formal role has changed. The recurring difficulty has been connecting a direction to the system, the team and the people affected by it. Leadership does not guarantee that an organisation survives, and a failed organisation does not make every contribution within it meaningless. The way people and work were treated determines what can still be learned and carried forward. A title can end while its consequences, relationships and example continue.
All of this can sound like the ramblings of a troubled mind. It is also why asking for help matters. Friends and family care for us when we are all out of love to give ourselves; they should not have to carry the consequences in silence.
When another opportunity arrives, the questions are personal again. Am I up for it? Will I make responsible and ethical choices when it gets too much? Am I willing to ask for help, rather than let the people closest to me carry a responsibility I refuse to name? Being bold is easier to admire from a distance than to live with every day.
It is a responsibility you earn, and you pay with scars. That is why I do not want exhaustion mistaken for having done it well. People often find enough time and money to do things twice. Would it not be better to take the time to do them properly the first time? There is no virtue in burning everybody out on the way. Straightforward, perhaps. Easy, no.

body:
Teachings of the mirror
A reflection written for Mahashivratri in February 2020.
There is a saying that the teacher appears when the student is ready. There is another that there is no knowledge without a teacher. What interests me is that the teacher can be formless. A person can teach, but so can an encounter that refuses to fit what I already believe. That was one of the largest things the preceding decade had taught me.
At the time, I looked forward to a day when I could retire as a professor. Every wakeful moment felt like part of becoming a good teacher. Before that, though, I had so much to learn and do. I did not want to hand future students a half-baked perception of reality. I wanted to bring them something factual, experiential and broad enough to have survived contact with more than my own explanation.
It was a long journey. I was in no rush.
A festival, and a teacher
Mahashivratri and Gurupurnima were the festivals I felt closest to. On Mahashivratri, alongside other devotees, I celebrated Shiva and his beauty. In the yogic legends, Shiva is Adiyogi, the first yogi and a great teacher. The figure drew my attention towards what a teacher might make possible.
Now, what does any of that have to do with a mirror? Mere ramblings of a madman, or an underlying symmetry? Of course I had a reason for going there.
A true teacher, in the ideal I was reaching for, is an unbiased observer who gives you methods for discarding the notions that hold you down. The teacher does not simply put a more impressive set of notions in their place. They help you see the choices that your account of yourself and society had made invisible. Like a mirror, they show you something you have to encounter for yourself.
The teacher can help reveal the path. Walking it remains your own doing. That was the meaning I found in Shiva's bhakti: a relationship that could liberate the seeker into discovery, while leaving the work of living with the seeker.
Methods in the middle of the chaos
Amid the chaos, I found myself reaching for methods rather than a rule for every possible situation. You follow a practice. Distractions and hurdles arrive. Your picture of reality changes as you make your way through it. Faith can keep you moving when the path is no longer as obvious as it looked from the beginning.
The mirror remains beside you. What it shows may be uncomfortable. There is no guarantee that the person you meet in it resembles the person you have been explaining to everyone else. The choice to respond to that encounter is yours. In this image, the methods do not change to flatter the person I would prefer to see. I am the one being asked to change.
That is a demanding image of teaching. It asks for more than passing on an answer. It asks whether I can help somebody examine what stands between them and their own understanding. It also turns the question back on me: what am I still unable to see because I need my present account to remain intact?
The difficulty of being the mirror
In ordinary life, I am hardly an unbiased observer. I have more biases than I can count and much to learn. Calling the teacher a mirror does not suddenly make me one. It makes the distance between the ideal and my own practice harder to overlook.
What I kept finding in the teachings of Shiva was an image of balance: an unbiased consciousness pervading existence. I found it almost poetic. Survival and exuberance are different ambitions. The habits that get us through a day may not be the habits that let us encounter it fully.
I did not know what God was, or whether God existed at all. I was still discovering things with every wakeful moment. Yet the idea of a supreme consciousness that could remain balanced and unbiased gave me something to contemplate. Seen through that ideal, the austerity associated with Shiva's path began to make sense to me. The simplest statement could contain an extraordinarily difficult way of living.
Back to the hazy borders
I returned to the borders between history, science, art, myths and legends. The festival gave me an occasion to stay with the questions, and to be grateful for the teachers I had already encountered. Their forms had been different. So had the things they made possible.
The aspiration to teach belonged to that moment in my life. The question it carried continues through learning with a real problem: what must I understand, and what support must I offer, before another person can make the work their own?
A mirror cannot take the journey for the person standing before it. It can make the next act of looking possible.
And be careful what you wish for. It just might come true. 😉

node.title: Gravity was still acting on the magnet
node.description: A first-decade reflection on the people, experiments and personal life that shape professional judgment.

body:
Gravity was still acting on the magnet
This reflection began in August 2024, looking back at my first decade of work. Its sense of standing at a turning point belongs to that moment.
I have been lucky in the people I have worked with. Academia, research, startups and communities put me beside minds that made me want to understand more. Who I would be working with often mattered more to me than what the work paid. That choice changed what I got to learn.
The work itself was rarely confined to the title. Cleaning the office floor, making PCBs, writing firmware, building a model, finding a vendor, supporting the customer, making a sale, raising money and helping a team grow could all belong to the same undertaking. A company starting from nothing does not politely wait for the correct department to exist.
I tried my hands at a great deal of it. As I thought you should. The first ten years seemed like a chance to discover what I was good at and what I was spectacularly capable of being bad at. Boy, did I use the opportunity.
An extensive period of regression testing
The experiments were not confined to work. I trained for MMA and entered tournaments, played piano, made art, hiked through different parts of India and spent time in monasteries. I read a lot, and bought more books than I could read. There were the pleasures and confusions of being in my twenties, too.
Eat, pray, love, if you want the familiar catalogue. I preferred to think of it as an extensive period of regression testing: eventually I might understand what all those Imtiaz Ali films had been going on about.
None of this fitted neatly around a career plan. It was the life in which the work was happening. A new interest could change the questions I brought back to an engineering problem. A difficult period could change how much I could carry, or what I thought was worth carrying. The person doing the job did not disappear when the job began.
Bread on the table, questions on the way
While I was discovering myself, I also had to put bread on the table. I joined Smart Joules as a founding engineer, moved into product development and support, worked as a product manager at Zenoti, and took part in ventures as an adviser, cofounder and consultant. The career journey follows those different responsibilities in their own settings.
Across them, artificial intelligence kept appearing. I had the good fortune to watch the distance between image-recognition work and language-model applications become part of ordinary product conversations. Being a nineties kid had already given me one version of that sensation: dial-up modems and floppy disks giving way to streaming on a phone. Suddenly the thing that had required effort and patience became something you expected to be there.
Timing mattered. I did not create the moment in which these possibilities arrived. I got to work while they were changing, and I got to learn from people trying to do something with them. I cannot tell that story honestly without saying how lucky I was.
The lessons also arrived outside the projects I was formally building. Presenting work, meeting someone after an event or sharing a few beers could open a conversation I would otherwise never have had. I learned from people just leaving college and from people who had spent more than forty years in industry. At barely thirty, I could learn from someone who had been doing the work longer than I had been alive.
Comparing those conversations, I kept coming back to leadership. Technical ability mattered, but so did how someone carried uncertainty, worked with other people and stayed with a problem. I was interested both in people who had made something work and people who had not made it work yet. That “yet” left room for the person to continue.
Two forces, one life
The analogy I liked was a pair of magnets dropped from a building. You might be studying gravitation, but electromagnetism has not agreed to stop operating for the convenience of your experiment. The magnets still attract or repel while they fall.
The professional and personal are like that. Calling one of them the subject of your attention does not suspend the other. The relationships, hopes and difficulties around the work still act on the person doing it. The work acts back.
In 2024, I felt myself reaching a turning point in both. I was imagining a life organised around more than my own next move. The decade behind me had felt like a sprint through experiences; I hoped the next one would become more of a marathon. I was projecting, of course. Time would have to tell me how well that description fitted.
But the possibility was already changing my priorities. I wanted to understand which parts of the first decade were experiments I had needed to try, which had become a practice worth sustaining, and what I would do differently if I began again.
That is where the next argument starts. The changing work of product management is one of the things those years taught me to care about. It comes from the engineering and the customers, certainly. It also comes from the people, the interests outside work and the life in which all of it had to make sense.

node.title: The future we create, and condemn
node.description: A January 2020 reflection on a father and son imagining the same future, the economics of making it real and the identities that shape our response.

body:
The future we create, and condemn
From January 2020. The original title was “The only way to be certain of the future is to create it. A surer way is to condemn it.”
What do we know about the past beyond the fact that it is not the present? Its ghosts haunt us, but so do the ghosts of the future's past: things that have not happened yet, which we already imagine remembering with regret. Somewhere between them, we can become the very thing we condemn.
If I wanted an image of collective consciousness, I would look at society. We are social animals, although we seem to have wandered very far into the woods around the tree of life. We create things we do not quite seek, then discover that they can organise our lives around themselves.
Welcome to capitalism, the unsaid religion of the twenty-first century. The comparison interested me because it concerned more than money. It concerned the arrangements through which we agreed that something deserved to exist, the things that received support and the questions that were easier to ask in favour of the arrangement than against it.
My father imagined this future too
My dad grew up with images of flying cars, personal robots and space. When I imagined a technological future, I kept finding some of the same objects there.
Roughly half a century separated the two imaginations. The intervening work mattered: science, engineering, manufacturing, markets and the effort of making a possibility usable. But the recurrence still unsettled me. Why could a technology remain vivid as an image for so long before it became part of ordinary life?
Capitalism solves problems, not bare-metal mathematics. A scientific possibility does not organise its own adoption. Someone has to find a use, gather resources and make the arrangement work. That is one place where the delay enters. The science is not thereby finished, nor the engineering merely waiting for permission; the path from an idea to a shared way of living has several kinds of work inside it.
People, society and nature keep introducing the variable or two that the projection left out. We might succeed in pulling one over the chaos. I would hesitate to make a plan on the assumption that the odds were permanently in our favour.
What receives the blessing?
Capitalism’s latest rebound, in the metaphor I was carrying, was STEM. I was glad to see science and technology attract resources. We needed the tree to bear useful fruit. We had left an extraordinary mess on the planet, and hoping that somebody else would eventually clean it up was hardly an adequate response.
Yet that was also the question. Were we solving the problem, or delaying it long enough for a later generation to inherit the bill? A more sophisticated way to move the burden could look like progress from the place where the burden had disappeared.
Philosophy and ethics seemed less fortunate in the competition for resources. They could ask what prosperity meant and who paid for it, yet struggle to make their own work economically sustainable. The profitable imitation of moral concern could fare better than the patient inquiry. That contradiction made me angry.
Calling capitalism a religion was my way of asking which concerns it could hear. If an ethical question had no clear way to make money, did it still have a place at the table? If it challenged the table itself, who would pay for the chair?
Silence is not peace
If capitalism could create a broad consensus around useful work, why not welcome it? Because consensus and peace were not always the same thing. People could be silent because they agreed, because they were exhausted or because the cost of speaking was too high.
The possibility of an all-seeing system concerned me for a similar reason. Convenience and coordination could become attractive ways to accept a power whose consequences were difficult to contest. Orwellian anxiety did not require every part of an Orwellian world to have arrived already.
We could continue fighting the wars of our forefathers in new institutions. We could also let corporations acquire a power over ordinary life that public debate struggled to understand. The question was not settled by declaring the institution benevolent or the technology inevitable. It returned to the room we had left for ethics, philosophy and dissent.
Education was central to that room. It produced the people who would lead every other institution, yet so often entered the discussion as an afterthought. I wanted education that was not captured by one partisan account, one soil or one school of thought. The work of examining an idea should not require swearing loyalty to it first.
Becoming what I condemn
A conversation brought the question closer to home. We were talking about the things we did, the things we did not do and the things we once thought we would never do. The response to what had happened was the part we could work on most directly. For much of the rest, we could try; we could not command the outcome.
Attachment, fear and jealousy could gather around an identity until insecurity began making its decisions. A society could do this too. People defended inherited accounts of themselves, and the defence reproduced the behaviour they condemned in others.
So we went looking for cheat codes. Ways to notice the trap before the next response completed it. The difficulty was that even the effort to escape could feed on the same pride and insecurity. I could become very attached to the identity of somebody who had overcome attachment.
That is where the long-lost art of listening mattered. It asked me to let something enter that my identity had already decided was unwelcome. Detachment and capitalism meet in that uncomfortable discovery: my response to the world is helping to make the world I will have to live in.
Too close to the blue pixel
We went looking, and I found myself thinking that we had been too close to the blue pixel to see the picture. An enormous conversation could be taking place while I argued with the one point nearest my eye.
The only way to be certain of the future is to create it. A surer way is to condemn it: respond from the same fear, reproduce the same arrangement, then recognise the thing I dreaded as something I helped make.
It was a provocation about participation, not a promise of certainty. What did I really know about the present? Enough, I hoped, to examine my response before sending another version of the same problem into the future.
